metadata.summary: This evidence-based update addresses systemic treatment for adults with cutaneous and noncutaneous melanoma. It covers neoadjuvant treatment for resectable disease, adjuvant treatment after resection, and treatment of unresectable or metastatic disease, with options differentiated by melanoma type, stage, and relevant biomarkers. The update draws on an updated systematic review and incorporates recommendations concerning uveal melanoma.

care_settings: Treatment of unresectable and/or metastatic melanoma
target_population: Adult patients with melanoma (cutaneous and noncutaneous)
therapeutic_areas: Systemic therapy for unresectable and/or metastatic melanoma

toxicities.event: Treatment-related adverse events before surgery in Dummer et al
toxicities.incidence: In Dummer et al, 5.5% of patients receiving T-VEC had grade 3 or worse treatment-related adverse events before surgery.
In KEYNOTE-716, grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 16% of patients receiving pembrolizumab versus 4% receiving placebo.
In CheckMate 76K, grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 10% of patients receiving nivolumab versus 2% receiving placebo.
In CheckMate 915, grade 3 and 4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 32.6% of patients receiving nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus 12.8% receiving nivolumab alone.

toxicities.event: Severe treatment-related toxicity and treatment discontinuation in adjuvant trials
toxicities.incidence: Reported severe (grade 3) treatment-related toxicity was 41% with dabrafenib plus trametinib, 14.4% with nivolumab, and 14.7% with pembrolizumab. Treatment discontinuation was 26% in COMBI-AD, 8% in CheckMate 238, and 10% in KEYNOTE-054.
In IMMUNED, grade 3 or greater treatment-related adverse events occurred in 71% of patients receiving nivolumab plus ipilimumab, 27% receiving nivolumab, and 6% receiving placebo.
In RELATIVITY-047, grade 3 or 4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 18.9% of patients receiving nivolumab plus relatlimab versus 9.7% receiving nivolumab alone.
In M14TIL, grade 3 or worse treatment-related adverse events occurred in 100% of patients receiving TILs versus 57% receiving ipilimumab.

recognition: Clinicians should remain highly alert to immune-related adverse effects during immunotherapy.
Even chronic grade 1 adverse effects, such as fatigue, can substantially impair quality of life.

management.actions: Discuss adverse effects and their longer-term management with the patient, particularly when care transitions to a family or primary care provider. The guideline directs clinicians to ASCO guidance for identifying and managing immune-related adverse effects.

toxicities.event: Immune-related morbidity with adjuvant treatment for stage II melanoma
recognition: Immune-related adverse effects can cause serious acute or long-term morbidity.

management.actions: Individualize the decision after discussing risks and benefits with the patient, weighing possible serious morbidity against the absence of overall survival data in stage II disease.

toxicities.event: Grade 3 and 4 adverse events with tebentafusp
toxicities.incidence: The guideline describes the frequency of grade 3 and 4 adverse events as substantial but provides no percentage.
OPTIM reported somewhat more grade 3 and 4 toxicities with T-VEC; no percentage is given.

therapies_index.name: pembrolizumab
approved_indications: The US Food and Drug Administration approves its adjuvant use after complete resection of melanoma involving lymph nodes.
The guideline recommends it as adjuvant therapy for resected stage IIB or IIC melanoma, resected stage IIIA-D melanoma, and as an option for resected stage IV melanoma.
The guideline recommends it as an option for unresectable and/or metastatic cutaneous melanoma.
therapies_index.administration: For neoadjuvant treatment, a maximum of 3 courses of 200 mg iv once every 3 weeks before resection, followed by a maximum of 15 courses of 200 mg iv once every 3 weeks after resection. An adjuvant schedule is 200 mg iv once every 3 weeks for 52 weeks. For unresectable and/or metastatic disease, listed schedules are 10 mg/kg iv once every 2 weeks or once every 3 weeks; 2 mg/kg iv once every 3 weeks; 200 mg iv once every 3 weeks; and 400 mg iv once every 6 weeks.
key_toxicities: In KEYNOTE-716, grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 16% of patients receiving pembrolizumab versus 4% receiving placebo.
Immune-related toxicity can cause serious acute or long-term morbidity.
monitoring: During longer anti–PD-1 dosing intervals, continue appropriate surveillance for toxicity and disease progression.

therapies_index.name: nivolumab
approved_indications: The US Food and Drug Administration approves its adjuvant use after complete resection of melanoma involving lymph nodes.
The guideline recommends it as adjuvant therapy for resected stage IIB or IIC melanoma, resected stage IIIA-D melanoma, and as an option for resected stage IV melanoma.
The guideline recommends it as an option for unresectable and/or metastatic cutaneous melanoma.
therapies_index.administration: An adjuvant schedule is 240 mg iv once every 2 weeks or 480 mg iv once every 4 weeks for 52 weeks. Listed schedules for unresectable and/or metastatic disease are 3 mg/kg iv once every 2 weeks, 240 mg iv once every 2 weeks, or 480 mg iv once every 4 weeks.
key_toxicities: In CheckMate 76K, grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 10% of patients receiving nivolumab versus 2% receiving placebo.
In IMMUNED, grade 3 or greater treatment-related adverse events occurred in 27% of patients receiving nivolumab versus 6% receiving placebo.
Immune-related toxicity can cause serious acute or long-term morbidity.
monitoring: During longer anti–PD-1 dosing intervals, continue appropriate surveillance for toxicity and disease progression.

therapies_index.name: ipilimumab
approved_indications: The US Food and Drug Administration approves 3 mg/kg once every 3 weeks for up to four doses for patients addressed by the guideline's recommendation on BRAF wild-type unresectable and/or metastatic cutaneous melanoma after progression on anti–PD-1–based therapy.
therapies_index.administration: For the approved post-progression indication described in the guideline, 3 mg/kg once every 3 weeks for up to four doses.
key_toxicities: In SWOG S1404, grade 3 or worse treatment-related adverse events were more frequent with ipilimumab and IFN than with pembrolizumab.
monitoring: Maintain vigilance for immune-related toxicity when administering immunotherapy.

therapies_index.name: relatlimab
therapies_index.administration: In combination with nivolumab, 160 mg iv once every 4 weeks until progression.

therapies_index.name: dabrafenib
therapies_index.administration: With trametinib, 150 mg orally twice daily; the listed adjuvant course lasts 52 weeks.

therapies_index.name: trametinib
therapies_index.administration: With dabrafenib, 2 mg orally once daily; the listed adjuvant course lasts 52 weeks.

therapies_index.name: encorafenib
therapies_index.administration: With binimetinib, 450 mg orally once daily.

therapies_index.name: binimetinib
therapies_index.administration: With encorafenib, 45 mg orally twice daily.

therapies_index.name: vemurafenib
therapies_index.administration: With cobimetinib, 960 mg orally twice daily without pause.

therapies_index.name: cobimetinib
therapies_index.administration: With vemurafenib, 60 mg orally once daily for 21 days of a cycle, followed by 7 days off.

therapies_index.name: tebentafusp
approved_indications: The guideline recommends it for HLA-A*02:01-positive patients with metastatic uveal melanoma.
therapies_index.administration: 20 mg once on day 1, 30 mg once on day 8, and 68 mg once weekly thereafter until progression.
key_toxicities: The guideline describes a substantial frequency of grade 3 and 4 adverse events, with toxicity becoming more manageable over time.

therapies_index.name: talimogene laherparepvec
approved_indications: The guideline permits it as primary therapy for patients with injectable unresectable cutaneous, subcutaneous, or nodal lesions who are ineligible for, or do not want, the recommended systemic treatments.
key_toxicities: In the OPTIM trial, grade 3 and 4 toxicities were somewhat increased with T-VEC.

therapies_index.name: high-dose IFN
key_toxicities: In SWOG S1404, grade 3 or worse treatment-related adverse events were more frequent with IFN and ipilimumab than with pembrolizumab.

therapies_index.name: atezolizumab
approved_indications: The guideline notes US Food and Drug Administration approval in 2020 for addition to vemurafenib plus cobimetinib on the basis of Imspire150; the Expert Panel does not recommend combinations of PD-(L)1 inhibitors with BRAF/MEK inhibitors.

therapies_index.name: selumetinib
key_toxicities: In Carvajal 2014, grade 3 toxicity was more frequent with selumetinib.

therapies_index.name: fotemustine
therapies_index.administration: EORTC 18021 compared administration through a hepatic intra-arterial catheter with intravenous administration in patients with uveal melanoma and liver metastases.

therapies_index.name: entrectinib
approved_indications: The US Food and Drug Administration approves it for unresectable and/or metastatic solid tumors with NTRK fusions after progression on standard therapies and/or when no other viable treatment exists; the guideline states that this indication includes qualifying patients with melanoma.

therapies_index.name: larotrectinib
approved_indications: The US Food and Drug Administration approves it for unresectable and/or metastatic solid tumors with NTRK fusions after progression on standard therapies and/or when no other viable treatment exists; the guideline states that this indication includes qualifying patients with melanoma.

therapies_index.name: nivolumab plus ipilimumab followed by nivolumab
approved_indications: The guideline lists it as an adjuvant option after resection of stage IV melanoma and as an option for unresectable and/or metastatic cutaneous melanoma.
therapies_index.administration: For resected stage IV disease: nivolumab 1 mg/kg iv plus ipilimumab 3 mg/kg iv once every 3 weeks for four doses, then nivolumab 3mg/kg once every 2 weeks for 1 year or until disease recurrence, whichever comes first. For unresectable and/or metastatic disease: nivolumab 1 mg/kg plus ipilimumab 3 mg/kg iv once every 3 weeks for 4 doses, followed by nivolumab 3 mg/kg iv once every 2 weeks, or nivolumab 240 mg iv once every 2 weeks or 480 mg every 4 weeks, until disease progression.
key_toxicities: In IMMUNED, grade 3 or greater treatment-related adverse events occurred in 71% of patients receiving the combination, versus 27% receiving nivolumab and 6% receiving placebo.
In CheckMate 915, grade 3 and 4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 32.6% with nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus 12.8% with nivolumab alone.
The guideline notes greater serious adverse-event risk with this combination than with other listed options.

therapies_index.name: nivolumab plus relatlimab
approved_indications: The guideline lists it as an option for unresectable and/or metastatic cutaneous melanoma regardless of BRAF mutation status.
therapies_index.administration: Relatlimab 160 mg and nivolumab 480 mg iv once every 4 weeks until progression.
key_toxicities: In RELATIVITY-047, grade 3 or 4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 18.9% with the combination versus 9.7% with nivolumab alone.

therapies_index.name: dabrafenib plus trametinib
approved_indications: The US Food and Drug Administration approves its adjuvant use after complete resection of melanoma involving lymph nodes.

The guideline lists it as an adjuvant option for resected stage IIIA-D BRAF V600E/K melanoma and resected stage IV BRAF V600E/K melanoma, and as an option for unresectable and/or metastatic BRAF mutant (V600) cutaneous melanoma.
therapies_index.administration: Dabrafenib 150 mg orally twice daily plus trametinib 2 mg orally once daily; the listed adjuvant course lasts 52 weeks.
key_toxicities: The guideline reports severe (grade 3) treatment-related toxicity of 41% and treatment discontinuation of 26% for dabrafenib plus trametinib in the adjuvant-treatment comparison.
The guideline notes that BRAF/MEK inhibitor combinations can have differing toxicity profiles.

therapies_index.name: encorafenib plus binimetinib
approved_indications: The guideline lists it as an option for unresectable and/or metastatic BRAF mutant (V600) cutaneous melanoma.
therapies_index.administration: Encorafenib 450 mg orally once daily plus binimetinib 45 mg orally twice daily.
key_toxicities: The guideline notes that BRAF/MEK inhibitor combinations can have differing toxicity profiles.

therapies_index.name: vemurafenib plus cobimetinib
approved_indications: The guideline lists it as an option for unresectable and/or metastatic BRAF mutant (V600) cutaneous melanoma.
therapies_index.administration: Vemurafenib 960 mg orally twice daily without pause plus cobimetinib 60 mg orally once daily in a cycle of 21 days with 7 days off.
key_toxicities: The guideline notes that BRAF/MEK inhibitor combinations can have differing toxicity profiles.

therapies_index.name: Neoadjuvant plus adjuvant pembrolizumab
approved_indications: The guideline recommends this perioperative sequence for clinical and resectable stage IIIB-IV cutaneous melanoma.
therapies_index.administration: Before resection, pembrolizumab for a maximum of 3 courses of 200 mg iv once every 3 weeks; after resection, pembrolizumab for a maximum of 15 courses of 200 mg iv once every 3 weeks.
key_toxicities: Immune-related toxicity can cause serious acute or long-term morbidity.

therapies_index.name: temozolomide plus cisplatin
key_toxicities: In the trial by Lian et al, grade 3 and 4 toxicities were similar between this regimen and high-dose IFN.

therapies_index.name: atezolizumab with vemurafenib and cobimetinib
approved_indications: The guideline notes US Food and Drug Administration approval of atezolizumab for this combination in 2020, while stating that the Expert Panel does not recommend combining PD-(L)1 inhibitors with BRAF/MEK inhibitors.
key_toxicities: The guideline considers increased toxicity likely with combinations of PD-(L)1 inhibitors and BRAF/MEK inhibitors.

therapies_index.name: pembrolizumab with dabrafenib plus trametinib
key_toxicities: The guideline considers increased toxicity likely with combinations of PD-(L)1 inhibitors and BRAF/MEK inhibitors.

therapies_index.name: spartalizumab with dabrafenib plus trametinib
key_toxicities: The guideline considers increased toxicity likely with combinations of PD-(L)1 inhibitors and BRAF/MEK inhibitors.

therapies_index.name: tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes
therapies_index.administration: The M14TIL trial required surgically resectable lesions totaling 2-3 cm in diameter to generate the cells.
key_toxicities: In M14TIL, grade 3 or worse treatment-related adverse events occurred in 100% of patients receiving TILs versus 57% receiving ipilimumab.

therapies_index.name: resection
approved_indications: The guideline places resection between neoadjuvant and adjuvant pembrolizumab for clinical and resectable stage IIIB-IV cutaneous melanoma.

therapies_index.name: local therapy
approved_indications: For asymptomatic brain metastases from melanoma, the cited joint brain-metastases guideline says local therapy may be delayed until intracranial progression if its listed systemic agents are used.
monitoring: Assess for evidence of intracranial progression when local therapy is delayed under the cited guidance.

recommendations.statement: Offer patients with clinical, resectable stage IIIB-IV cutaneous melanoma neoadjuvant pembrolizumab, up to three courses of 200 mg once every 3 weeks, followed by resection and adjuvant pembrolizumab, up to 15 courses of 200 mg once every 3 weeks.
recommendations.context: Type: Evidence based, benefits outweigh the harms.
recommendations.rationale: In SWOG S1801, delivering part of the pembrolizumab course before surgery improved event-free survival compared with giving the course only after surgery. Evidence for patients with stage IV disease was limited.

recommendations.statement: When feasible, offer patients with clinical, resectable stage IIIB-IV cutaneous melanoma enrollment in a neoadjuvant therapy trial or refer them for enrollment.
Offer adjuvant pembrolizumab or nivolumab to patients with resected stage IIB or IIC melanoma.
recommendations.context: Type: Evidence based. The nivolumab recommendation relied on a CheckMate 76K conference abstract and assumed that its findings would not be contradicted by the full publication. The choice should account for potentially serious acute and long-term immune-related toxicity and the absence of overall survival data in stage II disease.
recommendations.rationale: KEYNOTE-716 supported pembrolizumab through a recurrence-free survival benefit; the CheckMate 76K abstract supported nivolumab in the same population.

recommendations.statement: Do not offer adjuvant therapy to patients with resected stage IIA melanoma unless they are enrolled in a clinical trial.
recommendations.rationale: The guideline identified no positive trial results supporting adjuvant treatment for this stage.

recommendations.statement: For resected stage IIIA-D BRAF wild-type disease, offer either adjuvant nivolumab or pembrolizumab for 52 weeks, without ranking the options. Do not use ipilimumab or high-dose IFN routinely as adjuvant therapy.
recommendations.context: Type: Evidence based, benefits outweigh the harms. Patients with stage IIIA disease and microscopic sentinel nodal metastasis < 1 mm in diameter were excluded from the relevant randomized trials. Discuss individual risks and benefits with these patients, whose relapse risk is lower.
recommendations.rationale: Trials supported nivolumab and pembrolizumab, while indirect comparisons did not establish sufficient evidence to favor either. The guideline did not recommend routine adjuvant ipilimumab or high-dose IFN.

recommendations.statement: For resected stage IIIA-D BRAF-mutant (V600E/K) disease, offer adjuvant nivolumab, pembrolizumab, or dabrafenib plus trametinib for 52 weeks, without ranking these options.
recommendations.context: Type: Evidence-based, benefits outweigh harms. Patients with stage IIIA disease and microscopic sentinel nodal metastasis <1 mm in diameter were excluded from the relevant randomized trials. Individualize treatment after discussing risks and benefits with these patients.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence supports the anti–PD-1 options and dabrafenib plus trametinib, but direct comparisons among these options in this population are unavailable.

recommendations.statement: The guideline makes no recommendation either for or against adjuvant BRAF/MEK inhibitor therapy in resected stage III/IV melanoma with BRAF mutations other than V600E/K.
recommendations.rationale: Trials of adjuvant dabrafenib plus trametinib in patients with other BRAF mutations were not identified.

recommendations.statement: Offer adjuvant therapy to patients with resected stage IV melanoma.
recommendations.rationale: The Expert Panel reached consensus in favor of adjuvant treatment, although it could not strongly favor one option over the others.

recommendations.statement: Reasonable adjuvant options for resected stage IV melanoma are nivolumab alone, nivolumab plus ipilimumab followed by nivolumab, pembrolizumab alone, and, for BRAF V600E/K disease, dabrafenib plus trametinib.
recommendations.context: Type: Informal consensus. Evidence quality: varies by option; nivolumab alone: Moderate; nivolumab plus ipilimumab followed by nivolumab: Low; pembrolizumab alone: Low; dabrafenib plus trametinib: Low. Choice among options should involve shared decision making.
recommendations.rationale: The evidence for individual options is partly indirect or based on subgroups and gives no clear basis for strongly preferring one; the greater risk of serious adverse events with nivolumab plus ipilimumab warrants consideration.

recommendations.statement: For BRAF wild-type unresectable and/or metastatic cutaneous melanoma, offer nivolumab plus ipilimumab followed by nivolumab, nivolumab plus relatlimab, nivolumab alone, or pembrolizumab alone, without ranking the options.
recommendations.context: Type: Evidence based, benefits outweigh harms. Select among options with the patient after considering benefits and toxicity.
recommendations.rationale: The supported options differ in progression-free survival and toxicity; the combinations can offer greater progression-free survival benefit than single-agent treatment but increase toxicity.

recommendations.statement: As first-line treatment for BRAF-mutant (V600) unresectable and/or metastatic cutaneous melanoma, offer one of the following: nivolumab plus ipilimumab followed by nivolumab, nivolumab plus relatlimab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, dabrafenib plus trametinib, encorafenib plus binimetinib, or vemurafenib plus cobimetinib.
recommendations.context: Type: Evidence based, benefits outweigh harms. Discuss the choice of treatment with the patient. Recommendation 3.2.2 separately states a preference between nivolumab plus ipilimumab and BRAF/MEK inhibitor combinations.
recommendations.rationale: Trials support both the listed immunotherapy options and the listed BRAF/MEK inhibitor combinations in this setting.

recommendations.statement: Prefer first-line nivolumab plus ipilimumab over a BRAF/MEK inhibitor combination for BRAF-mutant (V600) unresectable and/or metastatic cutaneous melanoma.
recommendations.context: Type: Evidence based. Evidence quality: High for dabrafenib plus trametinib, Low for other BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Discuss the options and their risks and benefits with the patient.
recommendations.evidence_level: High for dabrafenib plus trametinib, Low for other BRAF/MEK inhibitors
recommendations.rationale: DREAMseq found better 2-year overall survival with a strategy starting with nivolumab plus ipilimumab rather than dabrafenib plus trametinib; extension of that finding to other BRAF/MEK inhibitor combinations rests on lower-quality evidence.

recommendations.statement: After progression on anti–PD-1–based therapy, patients with BRAF wild-type unresectable and/or metastatic cutaneous melanoma may be offered ipilimumab or an ipilimumab-containing regimen. Where feasible, offer or refer these patients for clinical trial enrollment.
recommendations.rationale: Direct trial evidence for ipilimumab after the recommended initial anti–PD-1–based regimens is very limited.

recommendations.statement: For BRAF-mutant (V600) unresectable and/or metastatic cutaneous melanoma, patients whose disease progresses after first-line anti–PD-1–based therapy may be offered a BRAF/MEK inhibitor combination described in recommendation 3.2.1. Patients whose disease progresses after a BRAF/MEK inhibitor combination may instead be offered anti–PD-1–based therapy described in recommendation 3.2.1.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence from treatment-sequencing trials supports activity in both directions, although those trials did not directly compare second-line options in patients who had all received the same first-line treatment.

recommendations.statement: Patients with injectable unresectable cutaneous, subcutaneous, or nodal lesions who are ineligible for, or do not want, the recommended systemic treatments may be offered T-VEC as primary therapy.
recommendations.context: Type: Evidence based, benefits outweigh harms.
recommendations.rationale: The guideline considers T-VEC an alternative for this limited population, not an equivalent option to the recommended systemic regimens.

recommendations.statement: Offer tebentafusp to HLA-A*02:01-positive patients with metastatic uveal melanoma: 20 mg once on day 1, 30 mg once on day 8, then 68 mg once weekly until progression.
recommendations.context: Type: Evidence based, benefits outweigh harms. The recommendation is not restricted to previously untreated patients.
recommendations.rationale: The trial by Nathan 2021 reported significant overall survival and progression-free survival improvements with tebentafusp compared with the investigator’s choice of treatment.

recommendations.statement: For patients with uveal melanoma outside the group addressed by recommendation 4.1.1, the guideline makes no recommendation for or against a specific systemic therapy. Where feasible, offer or refer these patients for clinical trial enrollment.
recommendations.rationale: The available evidence does not support selecting a specific systemic treatment for these patients.

recommendations.statement: In the absence of further data, patients with unresectable and/or metastatic mucosal melanoma may be offered the treatments described in recommendations 3.1 through 3.5. Where feasible, offer or refer them for clinical trial enrollment.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence specific to mucosal melanoma is limited; the Expert Panel based this option on its assessment of the indirect evidence for therapies used in cutaneous melanoma.

recommendations.statement: For other forms of noncutaneous melanoma, the guideline makes no recommendation for or against a specific systemic therapy. Where feasible, offer or refer patients for clinical trial enrollment.
recommendations.rationale: Randomized trials for these other forms were not identified, and the Expert Panel did not consider the evidence from cutaneous melanoma sufficient to recommend its treatments for them.

conditions.name: melanoma
conditions.description: The guideline addresses systemic treatment of melanoma in adults, including cutaneous and noncutaneous forms.
conditions.epidemiology: In some countries, melanoma incidence has risen by 3% annually. For the United States, 97,620 new diagnoses and 7,990 deaths were projected in 2023. Worldwide estimates for 2020 were 324,635 new diagnoses and 57,043 deaths.

subtypes.name: cutaneous melanoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The guideline separates treatment by resectability, stage, and BRAF mutation status.

subtypes.name: uveal melanoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Treatment of metastatic disease differs according to HLA-A*02:01 status.

subtypes.name: mucosal melanoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The guideline considers unresectable and/or metastatic disease separately from cutaneous melanoma.

subtypes.name: acral melanoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Patients with this form were included in the SWOG S1801 trial; the guideline gives it no separate treatment recommendation.

subtypes.name: spitzoid melanoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The guideline notes a higher prevalence of NTRK fusions in this form.

staging.system: eighth edition American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) criteria
staging.additional_rules: Unless stated otherwise, recommendations use the eighth edition. Some cited trials used the seventh edition, so benefit by contemporary stage III substage cannot be determined accurately.

long_term_effects: Immune-related toxicity can cause serious acute or long-term morbidity.
Persistent adverse effects, including fatigue, can substantially affect quality of life even when classified as grade 1.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Communication about lasting adverse effects should continue when care passes to a family or primary care provider.

conditions.name: cutaneous melanoma
conditions.description: The guideline distinguishes resectable disease, disease after resection, and unresectable and/or metastatic disease for systemic treatment.
conditions.epidemiology: The guideline reports a lower incidence rate of cutaneous melanoma in people with dark-pigmented skin than in those with light-pigmented skin.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Regional lymphadenopathy can be detected clinically in patients with known or suspected regional nodal metastasis. Disease may also present with cutaneous, subcutaneous, or nodal injectable lesions, or with brain metastases.

subtypes.name: resectable stage IIIB-IV cutaneous melanoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Clinical disease eligible for resection is addressed in the neoadjuvant recommendations.

subtypes.name: resected stage IIA melanoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Adjuvant therapy is addressed separately from that for resected stage IIB or IIC disease.

subtypes.name: resected stage IIB or IIC melanoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Adjuvant treatment is considered after resection.

subtypes.name: resected stage IIIA-D disease
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Adjuvant options differ by BRAF status.

subtypes.name: resected stage IV melanoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The guideline addresses adjuvant treatment after resection.

subtypes.name: unresectable and/or metastatic cutaneous melanoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Systemic options differ by BRAF status and prior treatment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish pathology and permit molecular characterization of suspected regional nodal melanoma.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Clinically detected lymphadenopathy in a patient with known or suspected regional nodal metastasis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline favors this approach over excisional biopsy, which has greater morbidity and is not routinely needed for these purposes.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Inform treatment selection because recommended options differ by BRAF mutation status.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When selecting systemic treatment for melanoma.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A BRAF wild-type result may rarely be falsely negative; repeat testing at progression could be considered, although the Panel identifies no high-quality supporting data.

genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: Mutation status affects selection of recommended systemic treatment.

The guideline cites an estimated prevalence of 0.2% in cutaneous melanoma and notes a higher prevalence in spitzoid melanoma. Testing may be reasonable when recommended therapies have been exhausted or no viable alternative remains.
Reported as a driver mutation, particularly in melanoma arising in sun-damaged skin; the Panel found insufficient treatment evidence for a formal testing recommendation.

special_populations.population: Patients with resected stage IIB or IIC melanoma
special_populations.considerations: Adjuvant treatment decisions should weigh the possibility of serious acute and long-term immune-related morbidity against the absence of overall survival data for stage II disease. The recommendation for nivolumab relied on a CheckMate 76K conference abstract at the time of writing, pending full publication that does not contradict it.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Adjuvant pembrolizumab or nivolumab should be offered, with treatment individualized after discussion of risks and benefits.

special_populations.population: Patients with resected stage IIA melanoma
special_populations.considerations: The guideline does not identify evidence supporting routine adjuvant treatment for this stage.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Adjuvant therapy should not be offered outside a clinical trial.

special_populations.population: Patients with stage IIIA disease and microscopic sentinel nodal metastasis <1 mm in diameter
special_populations.considerations: These patients were excluded from the randomized adjuvant trials discussed in the guideline. They have a relatively better prognosis and lower relapse risk than patients with greater sentinel-node involvement.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Adjuvant treatment should be individualized following a discussion of its risks and benefits.

special_populations.population: Patients with clinical and resectable stage IV disease
special_populations.considerations: The Expert Panel considered neoadjuvant treatment appropriate to offer, while acknowledging that evidence for this subgroup was sparse: SWOG S1801 included only 23 patients with stage IV disease.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Neoadjuvant pembrolizumab followed by resection and adjuvant pembrolizumab should be offered.

special_populations.population: Patients with resected stage IV melanoma
special_populations.considerations: The Expert Panel strongly favored adjuvant therapy but could not strongly favor one adjuvant option over another. Evidence for the individual options was indirect, derived from subgroups, or otherwise complicated; the adverse-event burden of nivolumab plus ipilimumab warrants consideration.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Options are nivolumab alone, nivolumab plus ipilimumab followed by nivolumab, pembrolizumab alone, and, for BRAF V600E/K disease, dabrafenib plus trametinib. The Expert Panel considered dabrafenib plus trametinib potentially more valuable when adjuvant immunotherapy cannot be given or tolerated.

special_populations.population: Patients with resected stage III/IV melanoma and BRAF mutations other than V600E/K
special_populations.considerations: The guideline found no trials of adjuvant dabrafenib plus trametinib in this population.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: No recommendation for or against adjuvant BRAF/MEK inhibitor therapy can be made.

special_populations.population: Patients with asymptomatic brain metastases from melanoma
special_populations.considerations: A separate joint ASCO, SNO, and ASTRO guideline addresses this population; it was not formally included in this update’s systematic review.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: That joint guideline states that ipilimumab plus nivolumab may be offered regardless of BRAF status, or dabrafenib plus trametinib may be offered for BRAF V600E mutation. If either is used, local therapy may be deferred until intracranial progression is evident.

special_populations.considerations: Performance status matters in treatment selection, although the guideline considers it less determinative for melanoma systemic therapy than for some other cancer regimens. Status impaired chiefly by tumor burden may improve after systemic treatment; impairment caused by comorbidities calls for careful assessment of treatment risks.

Concurrent conditions make treatment evidence harder to apply because trials may exclude affected patients. Clinicians should account for every chronic condition and the resulting uncertainty when planning treatment and follow-up, using shared decision making.

special_populations.population: Patients with unresectable injectable cutaneous, subcutaneous, or nodal lesions who cannot receive or do not want recommended systemic therapies
special_populations.considerations: The alternative depends on the presence of lesions suitable for injection.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: T-VEC may be offered as primary therapy.

special_populations.population: Patients with unresectable and/or metastatic melanoma harboring NTRK fusions after standard therapy or without another viable treatment
special_populations.considerations: The guideline notes an estimated 0.2% prevalence of NTRK fusion in cutaneous melanoma and a higher prevalence in spitzoid melanoma. The nonrandomized studies supporting the cited approvals included very few patients with melanoma; prevalence in noncutaneous melanoma is not well understood.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: NTRK fusion testing may be reasonable in the circumstances described, with larotrectinib or entrectinib offered if a fusion is found.

special_populations.population: HLA-A*02:01-positive patients with metastatic uveal melanoma
special_populations.considerations: In the trial discussed by the guideline, tebentafusp improved survival outcomes, although grade 3 and 4 adverse events were substantial and became more manageable over time. The guideline does not restrict its recommendation to previously untreated patients.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Tebentafusp should be offered at 20 mg once on day 1, 30 mg once on day 8, and 68 mg once weekly thereafter until progression.

special_populations.considerations: The guideline cannot favor or oppose a specific systemic treatment for patients outside the HLA-A*02:01-positive metastatic population addressed by its tebentafusp recommendation.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Enrollment in a clinical trial should be offered or arranged where possible.

special_populations.population: Patients with unresectable and/or metastatic mucosal melanoma
special_populations.considerations: Direct evidence is limited. The Expert Panel considered the cutaneous melanoma treatment recommendations applicable despite the absence of a universally accepted single staging classification for mucosal melanoma. Nonrandomized evidence suggests that KIT-positive disease may respond to imatinib, but the Panel considered the recommended cutaneous melanoma therapies more likely to benefit these patients regardless of KIT status.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Therapies described in recommendations 3.1 through 3.5 may be offered. Enrollment in a clinical trial should be offered or arranged where possible.

special_populations.population: Patients with other forms of noncutaneous melanoma
special_populations.considerations: No randomized trials were identified for these forms, and the Expert Panel did not consider it appropriate to recommend cutaneous melanoma regimens specifically for them.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: No recommendation for or against a specific systemic therapy can be made. Enrollment in a clinical trial should be offered or arranged where possible.

special_populations.population: Patients facing racial, ethnic, or geographic barriers to cancer care
special_populations.considerations: In the United States, racial and ethnic minority patients may face greater comorbidity burdens and obstacles to quality care; distance from treatment facilities can also restrict access. The guideline notes lower cutaneous melanoma incidence in dark-pigmented than light-pigmented skin, while African Americans are often diagnosed at noncutaneous sites, including mucosal and acral sites, or at a later stage.
The guideline recognizes potential oncology-care barriers including stigmatization, invisibility, and exclusion, and uses gender-inclusive language where possible.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with clinical and resectable stage IIIB-IV disease.
decision_rules: Offer pembrolizumab before resection, followed by postoperative pembrolizumab.
Offer enrollment in, or referral to, a neoadjuvant therapy clinical trial when feasible.

recommended_regimens.name: Neoadjuvant plus adjuvant pembrolizumab
recommended_regimens.summary: Administer pembrolizumab before surgery, resect the disease, and continue pembrolizumab afterward.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In SWOG S1801, 2-year EFS was 72% with neoadjuvant followed by adjuvant pembrolizumab and 49% with adjuvant pembrolizumab alone (difference, 23%; 95% CI, 11 to 35).
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Before resection: maximum of 3 courses of 200 mg iv once every 3 weeks. After resection: maximum of 15 courses of 200 mg iv once every 3 weeks.

not_recommended.name: Neoadjuvant T-VEC
not_recommended.reason: The Panel did not support its routine use because the Dummer 2021 trial was relatively small and had a high risk of bias that complicated interpretation.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence for stage IV disease was sparse: SWOG S1801 included only 23 such patients. The Panel made no recommendation for or against neoadjuvant nivolumab because it could not establish whether evidence for pembrolizumab could be applied to nivolumab in this setting.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with resected stage IIA disease.
decision_rules: Do not offer adjuvant therapy outside enrollment in a clinical trial.

not_recommended.name: Adjuvant therapy outside a clinical trial
not_recommended.reason: The guideline advises against offering it to patients with resected stage IIA disease.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with resected stage IIB or IIC disease.
decision_rules: Offer either adjuvant pembrolizumab or adjuvant nivolumab.
Individualize the choice after discussing the potential for serious acute and long-term immune-related morbidity against the absence of OS data in stage II disease.

recommended_regimens.name: pembrolizumab
recommended_regimens.summary: Adjuvant option following resection.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In KEYNOTE-716, the RFS HR for pembrolizumab versus placebo was 0.61 (95% CI, 0.45 to 0.82); twelve-month RFS was 90% versus 83%, and 18-month RFS was 86% versus 77%. OS data were not yet available.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 200 mg iv once every 3 weeks for 52 weeks.

recommended_regimens.name: nivolumab
recommended_regimens.summary: Adjuvant option following resection; at the time of writing, this recommendation relied on a CheckMate 76K conference abstract, assuming that full publication would not contradict it.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In CheckMate 76K, the EFS HR for nivolumab versus placebo was 0.42 (95% CI, 0.30 to 0.59); twelve-month EFS was 89% versus 79%. OS data were not yet available.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 240 mg iv once every 2 weeks or 480 mg iv once every 4 weeks for 52 weeks.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The Panel considered discussion of each patient's risks and benefits important despite the strong recommendation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with resected stage IIIA-D disease; treatment of stage IIIA disease with microscopic sentinel nodal involvement <1 mm should be individualized after discussion of risks and benefits.
decision_rules: Offer nivolumab or pembrolizumab as adjuvant treatment without ranking the 2 options.

Discuss the treatment choice with the patient. Patients with stage IIIA disease and microscopic sentinel nodal metastasis <1 mm were not included in the relevant randomized adjuvant trials and have a relatively better prognosis and lower relapse risk.

recommended_regimens.name: nivolumab
recommended_regimens.summary: Adjuvant immunotherapy after complete resection.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: CheckMate 238 found improved RFS with nivolumab compared with ipilimumab (RFS HR, 0.65; 97.56% CI, 0.51 to 0.83; P < .001).
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 240 mg iv once every 2 weeks or 480 mg iv once every 4 weeks for 52 weeks.

recommended_regimens.name: pembrolizumab
recommended_regimens.summary: Adjuvant immunotherapy after complete resection.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: EORTC 1325/KEYNOTE-054 found improved RFS with pembrolizumab compared with placebo (RFS HR, 0.57; 98.4% CI, 0.43 to 0.74; P < .001).
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 200 mg iv once every 3 weeks for 52 weeks.

not_recommended.name: ipilimumab
not_recommended.reason: Not recommended for routine adjuvant use; CheckMate 238 found better RFS with nivolumab than with ipilimumab.

not_recommended.name: high-dose IFN
not_recommended.reason: Not recommended for routine adjuvant use; the Panel concluded that the evidence did not support its recommendation.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Both recommended agents are FDA-approved for adjuvant treatment after complete resection of melanoma involving lymph nodes.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with resected stage IIIA-D disease; treatment of stage IIIA disease with microscopic sentinel nodal involvement <1 mm should be individualized after discussion of risks and benefits.
decision_rules: Offer nivolumab, pembrolizumab, or dabrafenib plus trametinib as adjuvant therapy without ranking the options.

Use shared decision making. Patients with stage IIIA disease and microscopic sentinel nodal metastasis <1 mm were excluded from the relevant randomized adjuvant trials and usually have a good prognosis and low relapse risk.

recommended_regimens.name: nivolumab
recommended_regimens.summary: Adjuvant option after complete resection.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 240 mg iv once every 2 weeks or 480 mg iv once every 4 weeks for 52 weeks.

recommended_regimens.name: pembrolizumab
recommended_regimens.summary: Adjuvant option after complete resection.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 200 mg iv once every 3 weeks for 52 weeks.

recommended_regimens.name: dabrafenib plus trametinib
recommended_regimens.summary: Adjuvant option after complete resection of BRAF V600E/K–mutant disease.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: COMBI-AD found significant RFS and OS improvements compared with placebo. Reported severe treatment-related toxicity was 41% with dabrafenib plus trametinib, compared with 14.4% with nivolumab and 14.7% with pembrolizumab in their respective trials.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Dabrafenib 150 mg orally twice daily plus trametinib 2 mg orally once daily for 52 weeks.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: There were no direct efficacy comparisons among these adjuvant options in this population. The reported discontinuation rates were 26% in COMBI-AD, 8% in CheckMate 238, and 10% in KEYNOTE-054.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with resected stage III/IV disease.
decision_rules: The Panel could make no recommendation either for or against adjuvant BRAF/MEK inhibitor therapy for this mutation group.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline identified no trials of adjuvant dabrafenib plus trametinib in patients with these other BRAF mutations.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with resected stage IV disease.
treatment_pathways.biomarker_condition: BRAF V600E/K is required for the dabrafenib plus trametinib option.
decision_rules: Offer adjuvant therapy, but do not prioritize a particular listed option over the others.
Select among the options through discussion with the patient, taking account of the higher serious adverse-event burden associated with nivolumab plus ipilimumab.
Dabrafenib plus trametinib may be particularly valuable when adjuvant immunotherapy cannot be given or tolerated.

recommended_regimens.name: nivolumab
recommended_regimens.summary: A reasonable single-agent adjuvant option.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In IMMUNED, median RFS was 12.4 months with nivolumab and 6.5 months with placebo; the RFS HR was 0.56 (95% CI, 0.33 to 0.94). Median OS was 43.2 months versus 31.9 months, respectively; the OS HR was 0.75 (95% CI, 0.36 to 1.56).
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 240 mg iv once every 2 weeks or 480 mg iv once every 4 weeks for 52 weeks.

recommended_regimens.name: nivolumab plus ipilimumab followed by nivolumab
recommended_regimens.summary: A reasonable combination adjuvant option, with its greater potential for serious adverse events considered during treatment selection.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In IMMUNED, median RFS was not reached with the combination, versus 12.4 months with nivolumab and 6.5 months with placebo. RFS HRs were 0.23 (95% CI, 0.12 to 0.45) versus placebo and 0.40 (95% CI, 0.20 to 0.79) versus nivolumab alone. Grade 3 or greater TRAEs occurred in 71% with the combination, 27% with nivolumab, and 6% with placebo. A stage IV subgroup of CheckMate 915 found no significant RFS improvement for nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus nivolumab plus placebo (HR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.58 to 1.32).
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Nivolumab 1 mg/kg iv plus ipilimumab 3 mg/kg iv once every 3 weeks for four doses, followed by nivolumab 3mg/kg once every 2 weeks for 1 year or until disease recurrence, whichever comes first.

recommended_regimens.name: pembrolizumab
recommended_regimens.summary: A reasonable single-agent adjuvant option supported by indirect evidence rather than a study in this resected stage IV population.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 200 mg iv once every 3 weeks for 52 weeks.

recommended_regimens.name: dabrafenib plus trametinib
recommended_regimens.summary: A reasonable adjuvant option for BRAF V600E/K disease, based on indirect evidence from stage III disease.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Dabrafenib 150 mg orally twice daily plus trametinib 2 mg orally once daily for 52 weeks.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The recommendation to offer adjuvant therapy has evidence quality Moderate and strength Strong; the choice among the listed regimens has strength Weak and evidence quality that varies by option. The trials of combination therapy produced mixed findings.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with unresectable and/or metastatic disease.
decision_rules: Offer any of the 4 listed systemic options without a prescribed order of preference.
Choose jointly with the patient after weighing benefits and toxicity; combination therapy may appeal to patients seeking a more aggressive approach.
For patients with brain metastases, the separately published ASCO, SNO, and ASTRO guideline identifies nivolumab plus ipilimumab as the most reasonable systemic option.

recommended_regimens.name: nivolumab plus ipilimumab followed by nivolumab
recommended_regimens.summary: Combination treatment followed by single-agent nivolumab; discuss its greater toxicity relative to nivolumab alone.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Nivolumab 1 mg/kg plus ipilimumab 3 mg/kg iv once every 3 weeks for 4 doses, followed by nivolumab 3 mg/kg iv once every 2 weeks; alternatively, follow the 4 combination doses with nivolumab 240 mg iv once every 2 weeks or 480 mg every 4 weeks, until disease progression.

recommended_regimens.name: nivolumab plus relatlimab
recommended_regimens.summary: Combination option for unresectable or metastatic disease.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In RELATIVITY-047, median PFS was 10.12 months with the combination versus 4.63 months with nivolumab alone (PFS HR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.62 to 0.92); estimated 12-month PFS was 47.7% versus 36.0%. OS was not yet reported.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Relatlimab 160 mg and nivolumab 480 mg iv once every 4 weeks until progression.

artifacts.title: Systemic Therapy for Melanoma Algorithm
artifacts.description: Step 1: For metastatic uveal melanoma with HLA-A*02:01 positivity, offer tebentafusp; for other uveal melanoma, offer enrollment in a clinical trial where possible without favoring a specific systemic therapy. Step 2: For cutaneous melanoma, determine whether resection is feasible. If clinical stage IIIB-IV disease is resectable, offer neoadjuvant pembrolizumab followed by resection and adjuvant pembrolizumab; also offer a neoadjuvant therapy clinical trial where possible. Step 3: After resection, do not offer adjuvant therapy for stage IIA outside a clinical trial. For stage IIB or IIC, offer adjuvant pembrolizumab or nivolumab. For stage IIIA-D with BRAF wild-type disease, offer adjuvant pembrolizumab or nivolumab; with BRAF V600E/K–mutant disease, also offer dabrafenib plus trametinib. For resected stage IV, offer adjuvant therapy; the options shown are nivolumab, pembrolizumab, nivolumab plus ipilimumab followed by nivolumab, and dabrafenib plus trametinib when BRAF V600E/K is present. Step 4: For unresectable or metastatic cutaneous melanoma with BRAF wild-type disease, offer nivolumab plus ipilimumab followed by nivolumab, nivolumab plus relatlimab, nivolumab, or pembrolizumab. After progression on anti–PD-1 therapy, ipilimumab or an ipilimumab-containing regimen may be offered. Step 5: For unresectable or metastatic cutaneous melanoma with a BRAF V600 mutation, offer those immunotherapy options or dabrafenib plus trametinib, encorafenib plus binimetinib, or vemurafenib plus cobimetinib. Prefer first-line nivolumab plus ipilimumab to a BRAF/MEK inhibitor combination. After progression on anti–PD-1 therapy, a BRAF/MEK inhibitor combination may be offered; after progression on a BRAF/MEK inhibitor combination, anti–PD-1–based therapy may be offered. Step 6: For patients with injectable unresectable cutaneous, subcutaneous, or nodal lesions who are ineligible for or do not want recommended systemic therapy, talimogene laherparepvec may be offered. Offer clinical trial enrollment where the applicable recommendations call for it.

document_sections.heading: ABSTRACT
document_sections.content: The guideline addresses systemic treatment decisions for clinicians caring for people with melanoma. An American Society of Clinical Oncology Expert Panel updated a systematic literature review, identifying 21 additional randomized trials. The update adds neoadjuvant pembrolizumab for resectable stage IIIB to IV cutaneous melanoma; adjuvant nivolumab or pembrolizumab for resected stage IIB-C disease; and adjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab as a possible option for resected stage IV disease. For unresectable or metastatic cutaneous melanoma, nivolumab plus relatlimab becomes a possible option irrespective of BRAF mutation status, and nivolumab plus ipilimumab followed by nivolumab is preferred to BRAF/MEK inhibitor treatment. Talimogene laherparepvec is no longer an option after progression on anti–PD-1 therapy in BRAF wild-type disease. Ipilimumab and regimens containing it are no longer recommended after progression on other therapies in BRAF-mutated disease. This full update also incorporates the uveal melanoma recommendations issued in the 2022 Rapid Recommendation Update.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: Melanoma systemic therapy has changed rapidly since ipilimumab appeared in 2011. During the subsequent decade, 12 new drugs gained approval for unresectable melanoma and four approvals were added in the adjuvant setting, while neoadjuvant research expanded. Overall survival and long-term survival improved substantially with newer treatments, but greater treatment choice and longer survival increased consultation time, patient costs, and societal costs. Rising incidence adds to the clinical workload; some countries have recorded annual incidence growth of 3%. For 2023, projections for the United States were 97,620 new diagnoses and 7,990 deaths. Worldwide estimates for 2020 were 324,635 new diagnoses and 57,043 deaths. These trends make evidence-based treatment selection important. ASCO developed its earlier systemic-therapy guideline in 2018 because melanoma carries substantial morbidity and mortality and therapeutic choices were changing quickly. Subsequent randomized trials addressed new agents, neoadjuvant treatment, earlier-stage disease, and uveal melanoma, prompting a full update.

document_sections.heading: THE BOTTOM LINE
document_sections.content: The central question is which systemic therapies provide clinical benefit to adults with melanoma. The population includes adults with cutaneous and noncutaneous melanoma; the intended readers are treating clinicians. Recommendations were developed by an Expert Panel using a systematic review. Unless specified otherwise, stages in the recommendations use eighth edition American Joint Committee on Cancer criteria.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: Recommendation 1.1: Offer patients with clinically resectable stage IIIB-IV cutaneous melanoma neoadjuvant pembrolizumab, up to three courses of 200 mg once every 3 weeks, then resection and adjuvant pembrolizumab, up to 15 courses of 200 mg once every 3 weeks (Type: Evidence based, benefits outweigh the harms; Evidence quality: Moderate; Strength of recommendation: Strong). Recommendation 1.2: Where feasible, offer or refer these patients for neoadjuvant clinical trials (Type: Informal consensus; Evidence quality: Not applicable; Strength of recommendation: Strong). Recommendation 2.1.1: Offer adjuvant pembrolizumab or nivolumab after resection of stage IIB or IIC melanoma (Type: Evidence based; Evidence quality: Moderate; Strength of recommendation: Strong). At the time of writing, support for nivolumab depended on the CheckMate 76K conference abstract and the assumption that its full report would not contradict it. Recommendation 2.1.2: Do not offer adjuvant therapy after resection of stage IIA melanoma except within a clinical trial (Type: Informal consensus; Evidence quality: Not applicable; Strength of Recommendation: Strong). Recommendation 2.2: For resected stage IIIA-D, BRAF wild-type disease, offer nivolumab for 52 weeks or pembrolizumab for 52 weeks without ranking them; ipilimumab and high-dose interferon are not recommended for routine adjuvant use (Type: Evidence based, benefits outweigh the harms; Evidence quality: High; Strength of recommendation: Strong). Recommendation 2.3: For resected stage IIIA-D, BRAF-mutant (V600E/K*) disease, offer nivolumab, pembrolizumab, or dabrafenib plus trametinib for 52 weeks, without ranking these choices (Type: Evidence-based, benefits outweigh harms; Evidence quality: High; Strength of recommendation: Strong). For recommendations 2.2 and 2.3, trials excluded stage IIIA patients with microscopic sentinel-node involvement <1 mm; these patients have a comparatively favorable prognosis and low recurrence risk, so discuss benefits and risks and individualize treatment. Recommendation 2.4: The evidence does not permit a recommendation either for or against adjuvant BRAF/MEK inhibitors after resection of stage III/IV melanoma with BRAF mutations other than V600E/K (Type: No Recommendation; Evidence quality: NA; Strength of recommendation: NA). Recommendation 2.5.1: Offer adjuvant treatment after resection of stage IV melanoma (Type: Informal consensus; Evidence quality: Moderate; Strength of recommendation: Strong). Recommendation 2.5.2: Reasonable choices are nivolumab alone (Evidence quality: Moderate), nivolumab plus ipilimumab followed by nivolumab (Evidence quality: Low), pembrolizumab alone (Evidence quality: Low), and, for BRAF V600E/K disease, dabrafenib plus trametinib (Evidence quality: Low); select through shared decision making (Type: Informal consensus; Evidence quality: varies by option; Strength of recommendation: Weak). Recommendation 3.1: For unresectable and/or metastatic BRAF wild-type cutaneous melanoma, offer, without a specified order, nivolumab plus ipilimumab followed by nivolumab, nivolumab plus relatlimab, nivolumab, or pembrolizumab (Type: Evidence based, benefits outweigh harms; Evidence quality: High; Strength of recommendation: Strong). Recommendation 3.2.1: For first-line treatment of unresectable and/or metastatic BRAF-mutant (V600) cutaneous melanoma, offer one of those four options or dabrafenib plus trametinib, encorafenib plus binimetinib, or vemurafenib plus cobimetinib (Type: Evidence based, benefits outweigh harms; Evidence quality: High; Strength of recommendation: Strong). Recommendation 3.2.2: Prefer first-line nivolumab plus ipilimumab to combined BRAF/MEK inhibition (Type: Evidence based; Evidence quality: High for dabrafenib plus trametinib, Low for other BRAF/MEK inhibitors; Strength of recommendation: Strong). Recommendation 3.3: After progression on anti–PD-1–based therapy in unresectable and/or metastatic BRAF wild-type cutaneous melanoma, ipilimumab or a regimen containing it may be offered; offer or refer patients to trials when possible (Type: Informal consensus; Evidence quality: Low; Strength of recommendation: Weak). Recommendation 3.4: For unresectable and/or metastatic BRAF-mutant (V600) cutaneous melanoma, combined BRAF/MEK inhibition may be offered after progression on first-line anti–PD-1–based treatment, and anti–PD-1–based treatment may be offered after progression on combined BRAF/MEK inhibition (Type: Informal consensus; Evidence quality: Low; Strength of recommendation: Weak). Recommendation 3.5: Patients with injectable unresectable cutaneous, subcutaneous, or nodal lesions who cannot receive or do not want the recommended systemic regimens may be offered talimogene laherparepvec as initial therapy (Type: Evidence based, benefits outweigh harms; Evidence quality: Low; Strength of recommendation: Weak). Recommendation 4.1.1: Offer tebentafusp to HLA-A*02:01-positive patients with metastatic uveal melanoma at 20 mg once on day 1, 30 mg once on day 8, then 68 mg once weekly until progression (Type: Evidence based, benefits outweigh harms; Evidence quality: Moderate; Strength of recommendation: Strong). Recommendation 4.1.2: No specific systemic treatment can currently be recommended for or against for other patients with uveal melanoma; offer or refer them to trials when feasible (Type: No recommendation; Evidence quality: Very Low; Strength of recommendation: Not applicable). Recommendation 4.2: For unresectable and/or metastatic mucosal melanoma, the Panel's consensus permits the treatments in recommendations 3.1 through 3.5 while further data are unavailable; offer or refer patients to trials where possible (Type: Informal consensus; Evidence quality: Very Low; Strength of recommendation: Weak). Recommendation 4.3: For other noncutaneous melanomas, no specific systemic treatment can currently be recommended for or against; offer or refer patients to trials when possible (Type: No recommendation; Evidence quality: Not applicable; Strength of recommendation: Not applicable).

document_sections.heading: THE BOTTOM LINE (CONTINUED)
document_sections.content: The continuation supplies recommendations 2.3 through 4.3, summarized in the preceding Recommendations section. Its qualifications emphasize individualized decisions for stage IIIA sentinel-node deposits <1 mm, shared selection among adjuvant and metastatic options, and trial access when specified. The document explains that evidence-quality and recommendation-strength definitions appear in Appendix Table A1 and encourages an opportunity for every patient to participate in cancer clinical trials.

document_sections.heading: FIG 1. Algorithm for systemic therapy for melanoma.
document_sections.content: The algorithm organizes treatment by uveal versus cutaneous melanoma, HLA-A*02:01 status in metastatic uveal disease, resectability, resected cutaneous stage, BRAF status, progression after anti–PD-1 or BRAF/MEK inhibition, and eligibility or preference for systemic therapy when injectable unresectable lesions are present. It displays the corresponding neoadjuvant, adjuvant, metastatic, and clinical-trial pathways and marks recommendation strength as Strong or Weak. For resected stage IIB or IIC disease, the Panel advises weighing potentially serious acute and long-term immune toxicity against the absence of overall-survival data in stage II disease and individualizing care. Stage IIIA patients with microscopic sentinel-node metastasis <1 mm were excluded from the pertinent randomized adjuvant trials; their relatively favorable prognosis and lower relapse risk call for individual risk–benefit discussion. A phase III trial found nivolumab plus ipilimumab followed by nivolumab superior to dabrafenib plus trametinib for the comparison marked in the algorithm. T-VEC denotes talimogene laherparepvec.

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: The guideline is based on systematic review and Expert Panel appraisal of evidence. Recommendation type, evidence quality, and strength are reported alongside individual recommendations.

document_sections.heading: Guideline Development Process
document_sections.content: A multidisciplinary Expert Panel included medical, radiation, surgical, and community oncologists, two patient representatives, and an ASCO staff member with health-research-methods expertise. It developed and reviewed recommendations using a published Cochrane review of metastatic cutaneous melanoma trials from 2016 or earlier, the review underlying the 2020 guideline, and an updated review of randomized controlled trials. The full update incorporates the 2022 Rapid Recommendation Update concerning tebentafusp in uveal melanoma. PubMed was searched on March 6, 2023, for publications dated June 1, 2019, or later. Eligible comparisons involved systemic therapy against another systemic treatment, observation, or placebo in any melanoma, with fully published randomized trials requiring at least 50 patients per arm; that arm-size restriction was absent from the original 2020 criteria. A Cochrane Central Registry of Controlled Trials search on May 12, 2022, used the same criteria. Randomized-trial meta-analyses were considered when they added information. Conference abstracts without peer-reviewed reports were principally used to anticipate possible recommendation changes, although specified exceptions informed recommendations. Editorials, commentaries, letters, news reports, case reports, and narrative reviews were excluded. Potentially eligible non-English articles could not undergo formal evaluation, but potentially pertinent references were retained. Trial quality was evaluated with methods based on the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool and elements of GRADE. For outcomes relevant to updated recommendations, evidence-quality categories were high, moderate, low, and very low. An implementability review found no concerns requiring changes. The public could comment on draft recommendations during a 2-week period; the Expert Panel, external reviewers, and the ASCO Evidence-Based Medicine Committee reviewed the recommendations before publication. ASCO plans to assess emerging literature to determine when another update is needed.

It cautions that additional schedules might subsequently have been approved.
