It notes that later approvals may provide additional dosing schedules.

document_sections.heading: Guideline Disclaimer
document_sections.content: ASCO presents the guidance as assistance for professional decisions, not an exhaustive treatment catalogue, an obligatory standard of care, or a replacement for judgment tailored to an individual patient. Evidence can change after publication. Recommendation wording conveys confidence about the net effect of an intervention while allowing individualized choices.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: The updated review found randomized evidence concerning multiple systemic treatments for cutaneous and noncutaneous melanoma.

document_sections.heading: Characteristics of Trials Identified in the Literature Search
document_sections.content: The update identified 21 relevant randomized controlled trials. The studies covered varied systemic treatments across cutaneous and noncutaneous melanoma. Trial quality, evidence strength, recommendation strength, and risk of bias were assessed. Earlier guideline trials and their results are summarized where pertinent. Additional reports on previously identified trials were generally not judged relevant to recommendation development unless the guideline says otherwise. Trials reported only as conference abstracts provide context or indicate possible future choices but ordinarily do not underpin recommendations; registrations lacking a published report or abstract are mentioned where later results could affect recommendations.

document_sections.heading: RECOMMENDATIONS
document_sections.content: Unless an exception is specified, staging in the recommendations follows eighth edition American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) criteria. ASCO updated the definitions used for evidence quality and recommendation strength after its 2020 guideline, including where the substantive recommendation did not change. Throughout this guideline, the shorthand nivolumab plus ipilimumab ordinarily means several combination cycles followed by a longer course of nivolumab alone; different schedules are identified when intended. Tables 1 and 2 provide recommended treatment schedules, and Figure 1 summarizes the decisions.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Question 1
document_sections.content: This question examines clinical benefit from neoadjuvant systemic treatment, alone or combined, in adults with resectable cutaneous melanoma and asks whether clinical characteristics or biomarker status modify benefit.

document_sections.heading: Summary of Updated Results for Question 1
document_sections.content: Two new trials were found. Dummer et al compared talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC) before surgery with surgery first in resectable stage IIIB-IV melanoma with injectable lesions; its risk of bias was considered high. SWOG S1801 compared neoadjuvant followed by adjuvant pembrolizumab against adjuvant pembrolizumab alone in resectable stage IIIB to IVC melanoma; its bias assessment raised some concerns.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 1.1
document_sections.content: Offer neoadjuvant pembrolizumab, no more than three courses of 200 mg once every 3 weeks, followed by resection and adjuvant pembrolizumab, no more than 15 courses of 200 mg once every 3 weeks, to patients with clinical and resectable stage IIIB-IV cutaneous melanoma (Type: Evidence based, benefits outweigh the harms; Evidence quality: Moderate; Strength of recommendation: Strong).

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 1.2
document_sections.content: Where feasible, offer patients with clinical and resectable stage IIIB-IV cutaneous melanoma enrollment in neoadjuvant clinical trials or refer them for enrollment (Type: Informal consensus; Evidence quality: Not applicable; Strength of recommendation: Strong).

document_sections.heading: Literature review and analysis.
document_sections.content: The 2020 guideline had identified four randomized neoadjuvant trials: Amaria 2018A compared neoadjuvant plus adjuvant dabrafenib plus trametinib with contemporary standard care; Amaria et al compared neoadjuvant ipilimumab plus nivolumab against nivolumab, with both groups subsequently receiving adjuvant nivolumab; Blank et al compared neoadjuvant plus adjuvant ipilimumab plus nivolumab against adjuvant combination alone; and OpACIN-neo compared two neoadjuvant schedules of ipilimumab plus nivolumab. None supplied sufficient support for a favorable neoadjuvant recommendation at that time. In the Dummer et al 2021 trial, T-VEC before surgery versus surgery first favored the neoadjuvant approach for RFS, HR 0.75 (95% CI, 0.58 to 0.96); EFS, HR 0.58 (95% CI, 0.44 to 0.78); and OS, HR 0.49 (95% CI, 0.30 to 0.79). Before surgery, 5.5% of T-VEC recipients experienced grade 3 or worse treatment-related adverse events. SWOG S1801 included resectable stage IIIBD/IV cutaneous, acral, and mucosal melanoma. Both arms received 18 total pembrolizumab cycles, with three given before surgery in the neoadjuvant arm. Its 2-year EFS was 72% with neoadjuvant plus adjuvant therapy and 49% with adjuvant therapy alone (difference, 23%; 95% CI, 11 to 35). Neither OS nor an EFS HR was reported.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Interpretation.
document_sections.content: For the 2020 guideline, the Panel regarded neoadjuvant treatment as investigational and encouraged trial referral. It identified core needle biopsy as the preferred diagnostic method for clinically detected regional lymphadenopathy in known or suspected metastatic melanoma: excisional biopsy is more morbid and generally unnecessary for pathology or molecular characterization. For the 2023 update, SWOG S1801 supports neoadjuvant pembrolizumab, with an EFS difference described as 23% fewer events at 2 years. Because both trial arms received the same total number of pembrolizumab cycles, the Panel saw little reason to expect additional harm solely from moving three cycles before surgery. Only 23 SWOG S1801 participants had stage IV disease; the Panel favored offering them neoadjuvant treatment while recognizing that evidence for this subgroup is sparse. Dummer 2021 suggested EFS and OS benefits from neoadjuvant T-VEC, but its 150 total patients, high risk of bias, and between-arm differences in surgery and adjuvant treatment complicate interpretation. The Panel therefore did not support routine neoadjuvant T-VEC. NADINA, a phase III trial, is studying neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus adjuvant nivolumab. The Panel knew of no similarly designed single-agent neoadjuvant nivolumab trial and could not agree that pembrolizumab evidence could be transferred to nivolumab in this setting; it made no recommendation either for or against neoadjuvant nivolumab.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Question 2
document_sections.content: This question concerns benefits of adjuvant systemic treatment, alone or in combinations, after resection of stage II, stage III, or stage IV cutaneous melanoma. It also considers whether clinical features, biomarker status, or lymph-node management distinguish groups with different benefit.

document_sections.heading: Summary of Results for Question 2
document_sections.content: The 2020 guideline described Seventeen randomized trials of adjuvant treatment in cutaneous melanoma. Most had low risk of bias, and concerns about the remainder did not warrant detailed comment. It also considered an individual-patient-data meta-analysis by Suciu et al of adjuvant interferon (IFN) versus observation or no IFN. The 2023 update found five additional randomized adjuvant trials—CheckMate 915, IMMUNED, KEYNOTE-716, SWOG S1404, and US Intergroup E1609—none rated at high risk of bias. The Panel also knew of a CheckMate 76K conference abstract.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 2.1.1
document_sections.content: Offer adjuvant pembrolizumab or nivolumab following resection of stage IIB or IIC melanoma; Table 1 provides reasonable schedules (Type: Evidence based; Evidence quality: Moderate; Strength of recommendation: Strong). The nivolumab recommendation relied, when written, on a CheckMate 76K conference abstract and assumes that a complete publication will not contradict that abstract.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 2.1.2
document_sections.content: Do not offer adjuvant therapy for resected stage IIA melanoma outside a clinical trial (Type: Informal consensus; Evidence quality: Not applicable; Strength of Recommendation: Strong).

document_sections.heading: Literature review and analysis.
document_sections.content: No positive stage II adjuvant trial informed the 2020 guideline. KEYNOTE-716 subsequently compared pembrolizumab with placebo after complete resection of stage IIB/C melanoma without regional-node involvement. Median RFS had not been reached in either arm; its RFS HR favored pembrolizumab at 0.61 (95% CI, 0.45 to 0.82). Twelve-month RFS was 90% versus 83%, and 18-month RFS was 86% versus 77%, respectively. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 16% with pembrolizumab versus 4% with placebo. OS results were unavailable. CheckMate 915 compared nivolumab plus ipilimumab with nivolumab plus placebo after complete resection of stage IIIB-D or IV melanoma. Neither RFS (HR, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.77 to 1.09) nor OS (HR, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.80 to 1.32) differed significantly. Grade 3 and 4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 32.6% with the combination versus 12.8% with nivolumab alone. In the CheckMate 76K conference report, nivolumab was compared with placebo after complete resection of stage IIB-C melanoma without regional-node involvement. Median EFS was unreached in both arms; the EFS HR favored nivolumab at 0.42 (95% CI, 0.30 to 0.59). Twelve-month EFS was 89% versus 79%, respectively, and grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 10% versus 2%. OS findings were not yet available.

document_sections.heading: Clinical interpretation.
document_sections.content: The absence of adequate stage II evidence had prevented a favorable adjuvant recommendation in 2020. KEYNOTE-716 now supports pembrolizumab in stage IIB-C disease because its RFS benefit is substantial and reasonably certain, although OS has not been reported; the Panel regards pembrolizumab adverse events as understood and manageable. CheckMate 76K supports nivolumab for the same population less definitively because only an abstract was available. Its design closely resembles KEYNOTE-716 apart from the agent and 2:1 assignment to nivolumab versus placebo. The Panel judged the reported EFS, RFS, and toxicity findings sufficiently similar, saw little reason to presume substantially poorer evidence quality, and weighed the risk of a premature recommendation against rapid obsolescence. Nevertheless, potentially serious acute and long-term immune-related morbidity must be balanced against absent OS data for stage II disease when individualizing care. The previous recommendation against adjuvant treatment was consequently limited to stage IIA disease, while a new recommendation addresses stage IIB-C.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 2.2
document_sections.content: For resected stage IIIA-D, BRAF wild-type melanoma, offer nivolumab for 52 weeks or pembrolizumab for 52 weeks without ranking the options. Ipilimumab and high-dose IFN are not recommended routinely as adjuvant treatment; use shared decision making and the schedules in Table 1 (Type: Evidence based, benefits outweigh the harms; Evidence quality: High; Strength of recommendation: Strong). Randomized adjuvant checkpoint-inhibitor trials excluded stage IIIA patients whose microscopic sentinel-node metastasis measured < 1 mm. Nivolumab and pembrolizumab are FDA-approved after complete resection of melanoma involving lymph nodes. Because stage IIIA involvement <1 mm carries comparatively better prognosis and lower relapse risk, discuss benefits and risks and individualize treatment.

document_sections.heading: Literature review and analysis.
document_sections.content: The earlier evidence included one meta-analysis and 14 stage III randomized trials not requiring a particular BRAF status. Three directly informed the relevant choices. EORTC 18071 found significantly improved RFS with ipilimumab versus placebo (HR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.64 to 0.89; P < .001) and OS (HR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.58 to 0.88; P 5 .001). EORTC 1325/KEYNOTE-054 found significantly improved RFS with pembrolizumab versus placebo (HR, 0.57; 98.4% CI, 0.43 to 0.74; P < .001). CheckMate 238 found significantly improved RFS with nivolumab versus ipilimumab (HR, 0.65; 97.56% CI, 0.51 to 0.83; P < .001). Later publication of complete US Intergroup E1609 results did not materially change its previously reported abstract findings. In SWOG S1404, pembrolizumab versus high-dose IFN or, after protocol amendment, ipilimumab significantly improved RFS (HR, 0.76; 99.62% CI, 0.59 to 0.99), but not OS (HR, 0.82, 96.3% CI, 0.61 to 1.09); grade 3 or worse treatment-related adverse events were more frequent with IFN and ipilimumab. Indirect comparisons by Toor et al and Longo et al did not estimate a statistically significant RFS difference between pembrolizumab and nivolumab: HR, 1.08 (95% CI, 0.78 to 1.49) and HR, 1.28 (95% CI, 0.84 to 1.94), respectively. Longo et al estimated an odds ratio of 2.13 (95% CI, 1.36 to 3.34) for grade 3 or 4 adverse events with pembrolizumab versus nivolumab. Although that study's supplementary material called the estimate a hazard ratio, the guideline treats that label as a likely error and reports an odds ratio.

document_sections.heading: Clinical interpretation.
document_sections.content: The Panel's 2020 appraisal did not support IFN, and the superiority of nivolumab to ipilimumab meant adjuvant ipilimumab was not the preferred immunotherapy. Nivolumab was supported by CheckMate 238 and pembrolizumab by EORTC 1325/KEYNOTE-054 together with comparable trial findings. SWOG S1404 further supports pembrolizumab as a reasonable option. The network meta-analyses do not establish a basis to prioritize pembrolizumab over nivolumab or vice versa, so recommendation 2.2 remains unchanged.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 2.3
document_sections.content: For resected stage IIIA-D BRAF-mutant (V600E/K*) melanoma, offer nivolumab, pembrolizumab, or dabrafenib plus trametinib for 52 weeks, without ranking these choices; decide jointly with patients (Type: Evidence-based, benefits outweigh harms; Evidence quality: High; Strength of recommendation: Strong). Randomized adjuvant trials of checkpoint and BRAF-targeted treatments did not include stage IIIA patients with microscopic sentinel-node metastasis <1 mm. All three options are FDA-approved following complete resection of melanoma with lymph-node involvement. The generally favorable prognosis and low recurrence risk when stage IIIA sentinel-node involvement is <1 mm warrant individualized risk–benefit discussion.

document_sections.heading: Literature review and analysis.
document_sections.content: The trials discussed for recommendation 2.2 also enrolled patients with BRAF-mutant melanoma. In BRAF V600 E/K disease, COMBI-AD found significant RFS and OS improvements for dabrafenib plus trametinib versus placebo. BRAF-mutant subgroup analyses of KEYNOTE-054 and CheckMate 238 suggested benefits similar to those in wild-type disease. No new trial in this population was identified for the 2023 update. An indirect network analysis by Sharma et al used BRAF-mutated subgroups of CheckMate 238 and KEYNOTE-054, all patients in EORTC 18071, and COMBI-AD; its reliance on subgroups limited patient numbers. Estimated RFS HRs were 0.88 (95% CI, 0.59 to 1.31) for dabrafenib plus trametinib versus nivolumab, 0.91 (95% CI, 0.57 to 1.44) for dabrafenib plus trametinib versus pembrolizumab, and 1.03 (95% CI, 0.67 to 1.77) for nivolumab versus pembrolizumab.

document_sections.heading: Clinical interpretation.
document_sections.content: Recommendation 2.3 did not change because no new trial evidence appeared. Anti–PD-1 treatment and dabrafenib plus trametinib are both reasonable options in BRAF V600E/K disease; COMBI-AD provides preliminary evidence of an OS benefit for the targeted combination. Without direct comparisons in this population, the guideline does not prioritize one approach; published network analyses support that position. Reported severe grade 3 treatment-related toxicity was 41% with dabrafenib plus trametinib versus 14.4% with nivolumab and 14.7% with pembrolizumab. Discontinuation was 26% in COMBI-AD versus 8% in CheckMate 238 and 10% in KEYNOTE-054.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 2.4
document_sections.content: The Panel cannot recommend either for or against adjuvant BRAF/MEK inhibitor treatment after resection of stage III/IV melanoma with BRAF mutations other than V600E/K (Type: No Recommendation; Evidence quality: NA; Strength of recommendation: NA). Neither the 2020 guideline review nor the 2022 update identified an adjuvant dabrafenib plus trametinib trial in patients with other BRAF mutations. Without such data, this treatment cannot be specifically recommended for them.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 2.5.1
document_sections.content: Offer adjuvant therapy to patients whose stage IV melanoma has been resected (Type: Informal consensus; Evidence quality: Moderate; Strength of recommendation: Strong).

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 2.5.2
document_sections.content: Reasonable adjuvant options after resection of stage IV melanoma are nivolumab alone (Evidence quality: Moderate), nivolumab plus ipilimumab followed by nivolumab (Evidence quality: Low), pembrolizumab alone (Evidence quality: Low), and dabrafenib plus trametinib for BRAF V600E/K disease (Evidence quality: Low). Choose with the patient after considering the available evidence (Type: Informal consensus; Evidence quality: varies by option; Strength of recommendation: Weak).

document_sections.heading: Literature review and analysis.
document_sections.content: For the 2020 guideline, CheckMate 238 was the only trial of nivolumab versus ipilimumab that included completely resected stage IV disease. The subsequent IMMUNED trial compared nivolumab plus ipilimumab, nivolumab plus placebo, and placebo in stage IV melanoma without detectable disease after surgery and/or radiotherapy. Median OS was unreached with the combination, 43.2 months with nivolumab, and 31.9 months with placebo; OS HRs were 0.41 (95% CI, 0.17 to 0.99) for combination versus placebo and 0.75 (95% CI, 0.36 to 1.56) for nivolumab versus placebo. Median RFS was unreached, 12.4 months, and 6.5 months, respectively. RFS HRs were 0.23 (95% CI, 0.12 to 0.45) for combination versus placebo, 0.56 (95% CI, 0.33 to 0.94) for nivolumab versus placebo, and 0.40 (95% CI, 0.20 to 0.79) for combination versus nivolumab. Twelve-month RFS was 75%, 52%, and 32%, respectively. Grade 3 or greater treatment-related adverse events occurred in 71% with combination, 27% with nivolumab, and 6% with placebo. A CheckMate 915 subgroup contained 245 patients with completely resected stage IV disease; RFS did not differ significantly between nivolumab plus ipilimumab and nivolumab plus placebo (HR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.58 to 1.32).

document_sections.heading: Clinical interpretation.
document_sections.content: The Panel agreed strongly on offering adjuvant treatment after resection of stage IV disease but could not strongly favor any one regimen because evidence was indirect, subgroup-based, or otherwise complicated. CheckMate 238 supports nivolumab alone at moderate evidence quality because stage IV patients were only a subset. IMMUNED, a small phase II study judged at low risk of bias, associated nivolumab plus ipilimumab with longer RFS than either placebo or nivolumab. Taken together with CheckMate 915 and stage III findings, however, the evidence for the combination is low quality: it probably has the highest serious-adverse-event rate among the options, and the larger CheckMate 915 stage IV subgroup of 245 patients found no RFS improvement over nivolumab, unlike the relevant IMMUNED arms comprising 115 patients; dosing and schedules also differed. Patients and clinicians should account for the greater adverse-event burden. Pembrolizumab was not studied directly in this population but is a reasonable nivolumab alternative by indirect extrapolation, yielding low-quality evidence. Evidence from stage III supports considering dabrafenib plus trametinib for BRAF V600E/K disease, also at low quality because it is indirect; it may be especially valuable when adjuvant immunotherapy cannot be given or tolerated. The 2020 guideline separately discussed stage III presentations, sentinel-node practice, recurrence risk, and molecular testing; that detailed discussion is not repeated here.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Question 3
document_sections.content: This question addresses beneficial systemic therapies, alone or combined, for adults with unresectable and/or metastatic cutaneous melanoma and asks whether features such as biomarkers or brain metastases affect benefit.

document_sections.heading: Summary of Results
document_sections.content: The main pre-2020 evidence source was a Cochrane review of metastatic-melanoma randomized controlled trials through October 2017, covering 122 trials and multiple meta-analyses. The earlier guideline identified nine additional randomized phase III trials, of which five were relevant to recommendations: Ascierto et al, CheckMate 511, COLUMBUS, NEMO, and OPTiM. All but the Ugarel et al trial were judged at low risk of bias. The 2023 update found Twelve new randomized trials of unresectable or metastatic cutaneous melanoma. Four—KEYNOTE-029, Lebbe´ et al, MIRACULUM, and SWOG S1320—were not treated as relevant to the recommendations in this summary. Additional reports from trials already identified in the earlier guideline or Cochrane review were not considered relevant to recommendation development.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 3.1
document_sections.content: Offer patients with unresectable and/or metastatic BRAF wild-type cutaneous melanoma any of the following without ranking them: nivolumab plus ipilimumab followed by nivolumab, nivolumab plus relatlimab, nivolumab alone, or pembrolizumab alone. Use shared decision making and the schedules in Table 2 (Type: Evidence based, benefits outweigh harms; Evidence quality: High; Strength of recommendation: Strong).

document_sections.heading: Literature review and analysis.
document_sections.content: In the Cochrane review, anti–PD-1 versus anti–CTLA-4 treatment was associated with statistically significant improvements in OS (HR, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.60 to 0.66; one trial) and PFS (HR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.50 to 0.60; two trials), and fewer grade 3 and 4 toxicities (RR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.54 to 0.91; two trials). CheckMate 067 and KEYNOTE-006 principally drove those findings. Combined anti–PD-1 plus anti–CTLA-4 treatment versus anti–CTLA-4 alone was associated with better PFS (HR, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.35 to 0.46; two trials) and reported increased grade 3 and 4 toxicities (RR, 1.57; 95% CI, 0.85 to 2.92; two trials). CheckMate 511 investigated alternative nivolumab plus ipilimumab dosing; Ascierto et al investigated higher-dose ipilimumab alone. The update identified two relevant fully published trials in BRAF wild-type disease. RELATIVITY-047 compared relatlimab plus nivolumab with nivolumab in previously untreated unresectable or metastatic stage III-IV melanoma. Median PFS was 10.12 months versus 4.63 months; PFS HR was 0.75 (95% CI, 0.62 to 0.92); estimated 12-month PFS was 47.7% versus 36.0%. OS had not been reported. Grade 3 or 4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 18.9% versus 9.7%. IMSpire170 compared cobimetinib plus atezolizumab against pembrolizumab in unresectable or metastatic BRAF wild-type melanoma and found no significant PFS or OS difference. An exploratory network meta-analysis suggested better estimated PFS with the two-drug combinations nivolumab plus ipilimumab and relatlimab plus nivolumab than with pembrolizumab or nivolumab alone; it estimated the highest serious-adverse-event frequency with nivolumab plus ipilimumab and the lowest with nivolumab alone. Its limitations preclude treating those estimates as high-certainty grounds for recommendations.

document_sections.heading: Clinical interpretation.
document_sections.content:
The 2020 guideline supported nivolumab and pembrolizumab monotherapy because CheckMate 067 and KEYNOTE-006 showed significant OS benefit for anti–PD-1 treatment over ipilimumab. CheckMate 067 was not powered to compare nivolumab plus ipilimumab directly against nivolumab alone; it found improved PFS with combination, a nonsignificant OS difference, and significantly greater toxicity. The combination was therefore considered reasonable for patients willing to accept likely higher toxicity. The PFS finding in RELATIVITY-047 similarly supports nivolumab plus relatlimab as another reasonable choice. Alternative schedules assessed in CheckMate 511 and higher-dose ipilimumab assessed by Ascierto et al were not recommended in the 2020 guideline. IMSpire170 found no benefit for atezolizumab plus cobimetinib over pembrolizumab. All four recommended choices should be discussed jointly with patients: combinations offer greater PFS benefit than nivolumab alone but more toxicity, and indirect evidence suggests a similar trade-off relative to pembrolizumab alone. The separate joint ASCO, SNO, and ASTRO brain-metastases guideline regards nivolumab plus ipilimumab as the most reasonable systemic choice for asymptomatic brain metastases on the basis of a phase II trial. Patients preferring more aggressive treatment may favor a combination. In pertinent trials, nivolumab could continue beyond 2 years whereas pembrolizumab was limited to 2 years. Courses as short as 1 year might be reasonable, but high-quality melanoma data do not establish the correct treatment duration. Longer dosing intervals, including up to 6 weeks, still require monitoring for toxicity and progression.

Earlier guidance noted that trials permitted nivolumab beyond 2 years, whereas pembrolizumab was restricted to 2 years. Treatment lasting as little as 1 year might be reasonable, but high-quality melanoma data do not establish the appropriate duration. Longer dosing intervals, such as up to 6 weeks, still require monitoring for toxicity and progression.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 3.2.1
document_sections.content: Patients with BRAF mutant (V600) unresectable and/or metastatic cutaneous melanoma should be offered one of these first-line options: nivolumab plus ipilimumab followed by nivolumab, nivolumab plus relatlimab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, dabrafenib plus trametinib, encorafenib plus binimetinib, or vemurafenib plus cobimetinib. Treatment selection should involve shared decision making; Table 2 presents dosing and schedules. Type: Evidence based, benefits outweigh harms; Evidence quality: High; Strength of recommendation: Strong.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 3.2.2
document_sections.content: As first-line treatment, nivolumab plus ipilimumab is preferred to a BRAF/MEK inhibitor combination. The choice should be discussed with the patient. Type: Evidence based; Evidence quality: High for dabrafenib plus trametinib, Low for other BRAF/MEK inhibitors; Strength of recommendation: Strong.

document_sections.heading: Literature review and evidence.
document_sections.content: The Cochrane review found that combined BRAF and MEK inhibition, compared with a BRAF inhibitor alone in BRAF-mutant metastatic melanoma, significantly improved OS (HR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.59 to 0.82; four trials) and PFS (HR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.44 to 0.71; four trials). Grade 3 and 4 toxicity rates were similar (RR, 1.01; 95% CI, 0.85 to 1.20; four trials). The contributing studies included coBRIM, COMBI-D, COMBI-V, and the trial by Flaherty et al. In COLUMBUS, encorafenib plus binimetinib significantly improved PFS relative to vemurafenib (HR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.41 to 0.71), but not relative to encorafenib (HR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.56 to 1.00); OS also differed significantly versus vemurafenib (HR, 0.61; 95% CI, 0.47 to 0.79). Grade 3 and 4 toxicities occurred at similar rates across its three arms. RELATIVITY-047 included patients irrespective of BRAF status. Four new randomized trials addressed BRAF-mutated disease. SWOG S1320 found no benefit from intermittent rather than continuous dabrafenib plus trametinib. Three trials added a PD-L1 inhibitor to BRAF/MEK inhibition. In Imspire150, adding atezolizumab to vemurafenib and cobimetinib improved investigator-assessed PFS (HR 0.78; 95% CI, 0.63 to 0.97), but not OS (HR 0.85; 95% CI, 0.64 to 1.11); independent review found no PFS difference (HR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.67 to 1.07). Reported severe toxicity rates were similar, although 22 patients assigned to the triplet stopped treatment during cycle 1 before receiving atezolizumab and were counted in the placebo safety population, potentially favoring the atezolizumab arm's toxicity estimate. KEYNOTE-022 initially found no significant PFS difference when pembrolizumab rather than placebo was added to dabrafenib plus trametinib (HR 0.66; 95% CI, 0.40 to 1.07). Its later report gave a PFS HR of 0.58 (95% CI, 0.34 to 0.83) and an OS HR of 0.64 (95% CI, 0.38 to 1.06), but its authors did not regard the PFS result as statistically significant given the trial design. COMBI-I found no significant PFS (HR 0.82; 95% CI, 0.66 to 1.03) or OS difference (HR 0.79; 95% CI, 0.59 to 1.05) when spartalizumab replaced placebo alongside dabrafenib plus trametinib. DREAMseq compared sequences beginning with nivolumab plus ipilimumab or dabrafenib plus trametinib. Because proportional hazards were not expected, its primary outcome was the 2-year OS rate: 71.8% with nivolumab plus ipilimumab first versus 51.5% with dabrafenib plus trametinib first; the difference was significant (log-rank P 5 .01). First-line median PFS was 11.8 months versus 8.5 months, respectively (log rank P 5 .054). SECOMBIT examined sequences involving encorafenib plus binimetinib and was designed as noncomparative, making its HRs and confidence intervals exploratory. It also included an arm receiving 8 weeks of encorafenib plus binimetinib before nivolumab plus ipilimumab. No significant PFS (HR, 0.71; 95% CI, 0.44 to 1.14) or OS difference (HR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.42 to 1.26) was reported. An exploratory network meta-analysis suggested that adding a PD-L1 inhibitor to BRAF/MEK inhibition might improve PFS but increase serious adverse events relative to the listed two-drug regimens and single-agent anti–PD-1 therapies. It also suggested that BRAF/MEK combinations might cause more serious adverse events than nivolumab, pembrolizumab, or nivolumab plus relatlimab, but not more than nivolumab plus ipilimumab. BRAF/MEK combinations could not be distinguished by PFS or adverse events. Nivolumab alone might have both the lowest PFS and the lowest serious-adverse-event frequency among analyzed options. The analysis's limitations prevent these suggestions from serving as good evidence for recommendations; they remain research questions.

document_sections.heading: Clinical interpretation.
document_sections.content: Evidence reviewed for the 2020 guideline established superiority over BRAF inhibition alone for vemurafenib plus cobimetinib in CoBRIM, dabrafenib plus trametinib in COMBI-D and COMBI-V, and encorafenib plus binimetinib in COLUMBUS. These are reasonable options for BRAF V600E/K–mutant melanoma alongside the treatments in recommendation 3.1. Evidence for adding a PD-(L)1 inhibitor to a BRAF/MEK combination remains difficult to interpret: the investigator and independent PFS assessments differed in Imspire150, while the apparent KEYNOTE-022 benefit emerged only after extended follow-up in a trial its authors said was not intended to be comparative. Although the US FDA approved atezolizumab for this indication in 2020 on the basis of Imspire150, the Panel does not recommend any PD-(L)1 inhibitor plus BRAF/MEK inhibitor combination because benefit evidence is limited and toxicity is likely greater. Recommendation 3.2.1 contains seven strongly recommended choices, but evidence for ranking them is mixed. DREAMseq favored a sequence starting with nivolumab plus ipilimumab over one starting with dabrafenib plus trametinib for 2-year OS. RELATIVITY-047 favored nivolumab plus relatlimab over nivolumab for PFS, without establishing how it compares with BRAF/MEK combinations; the exploratory network analysis did not settle treatment priority. Panel members differed on whether DREAMseq justified naming a preferred first-line treatment. Consensus ultimately favored nivolumab plus ipilimumab over BRAF/MEK inhibition: evidence was High for the comparison with dabrafenib plus trametinib and Low when extrapolated to other combinations, given SECOMBIT's noncomparative design and the absence of a comparable vemurafenib plus cobimetinib trial. The joint ASCO-SNO-ASTRO brain-metastases guideline recommends nivolumab plus ipilimumab for patients with brain metastases. Patients with better performance status or greater capacity to tolerate toxicity may prefer combination treatment over single-agent anti–PD-1 therapy, although that consideration does not resolve the choice between nivolumab plus relatlimab and a BRAF/MEK combination. Decisions should be shared with patients after weighing benefits and harms. Earlier guidance suggested that switching BRAF/MEK combinations because of toxicity might be reasonable because their toxicity profiles can differ; prospective evidence on switching after BRAF/MEK failure is lacking. Longer anti–PD-1 dosing intervals, such as up to 6 weeks, still require toxicity and progression monitoring.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 3.3
document_sections.content: Following progression on anti–PD-1–based treatment, patients with unresectable and/or metastatic BRAF wild-type cutaneous melanoma may receive ipilimumab or an ipilimumab-containing regimen. Where feasible, they should also be offered clinical-trial enrollment or referral. Type: Informal consensus; Evidence quality: Low; Strength of recommendation: Weak.

document_sections.heading: Literature review and analysis.
document_sections.content: Neither the 2020 review nor this update found trials directly addressing later-line treatment after the first-line regimens recommended in 3.1 for BRAF wild-type unresectable and/or metastatic melanoma. A trial identified by the Cochrane review studied second-line ipilimumab after chemotherapy or interleukin-2 (IL-2), rather than after anti–PD-1 therapy, limiting its relevance here.

document_sections.heading: Clinical interpretation.
document_sections.content: Compared with a vaccine control, ipilimumab was associated with improved OS and manageable toxicity after chemotherapy or IL-2. Evidence for its effectiveness after relapse on the recommended anti–PD-1–based first-line regimens is nevertheless very limited. In the absence of direct trials, Panel consensus permits ipilimumab or ipilimumab-containing regimens. US FDA approval of ipilimumab at 3 mg/kg once every 3 weeks for up to four doses in this setting rests on the trial by Hodi et al. An ipilimumab-containing option could include nivolumab plus ipilimumab after progression on single-agent nivolumab or pembrolizumab. The clinical-trial referral statement was added after external review. M14TIL compared tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) with ipilimumab after prior systemic treatment; TILs were outside this guideline's review scope. TIL treatment required surgically removable lesions totaling 2-3 cm in diameter. All but 4 of 168 participants had received anti–PD-1 therapy, including 40 in the adjuvant setting and 105 as first-line metastatic treatment. PFS favored TILs significantly (7.2 months v 3.1 months; HR, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.35 to 0.72). OS did not differ significantly (median 25.8 months with TILs v 18.9 months with ipilimumab; HR, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.54 to 1.27). Grade 3 or worse TRAEs occurred in 100% on TIL and 57% on ipilimumab; TIL recipients generally reported better health-related quality-of-life scores. The 2020 recommendation had included T-VEC on indirect OPTIM evidence. Additional indirect MASTERKEY-265 evidence led the Panel to remove T-VEC as an option after anti–PD-1 progression.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 3.4
document_sections.content: After progression on first-line anti–PD-1–based therapy, patients with BRAF mutant (V600) unresectable and/or metastatic cutaneous melanoma may receive one of the BRAF/MEK combinations described in recommendation 3.2.1. After progression on a BRAF/MEK combination, they may instead receive anti–PD-1–based treatment described there. Type: Informal consensus; Evidence quality: Low; Strength of recommendation: Weak.

document_sections.heading: Literature review and analysis.
document_sections.content: The 2020 guideline found only two randomized later-line trials including patients with BRAF-mutant unresectable and/or metastatic disease previously treated with an option in recommendation 3.2.1. KEYNOTE-002 enrolled only 125 patients with BRAF-mutant disease. Its prespecified subgroup analysis showed a PFS benefit versus chemotherapy with pembrolizumab 10 mg/kg once every three weeks (HR, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.26 to 0.74), but not with pembrolizumab 3 mg/kg once every three weeks (HR, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.46 to 1.18). The proportions previously receiving BRAF/MEK inhibition or ipilimumab-based treatment were unclear. In KEYNOTE-006, the subgroup previously exposed to BRAF inhibition had a PFS benefit with pembrolizumab every 2 weeks versus ipilimumab (HR, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.34 to 0.97), but not with pembrolizumab every 3 weeks. CheckMate 037 included later-line patients with BRAF-mutant disease but required progression after both anti–CTLA-4 and anti-BRAF treatment; whether any had received a recommended 3.2 option is unclear. Subsequently published DREAMseq and SECOMBIT results are discussed with recommendation 3.2.

document_sections.heading: Clinical interpretation.
document_sections.content: The 2020 Panel considered treatment after relapse reasonable despite little direct evidence beyond small subgroups, relying on first-line efficacy evidence and the absence of known cross-resistance. DREAMseq and SECOMBIT studied treatment sequences rather than randomizing patients with the same prior first-line treatment among second-line options. Their evidence of activity in both treatment orders led the Panel to remove ipilimumab and ipilimumab-containing regimens as reasonable choices after first-line progression. Although recommendation 3.4 does not name it explicitly, nivolumab plus relatlimab becomes a potential post–BRAF/MEK option through its inclusion in recommendation 3.2.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 3.5
document_sections.content: For patients with unresectable injectable cutaneous, subcutaneous, or nodal lesions who cannot receive or do not want the recommended systemic treatments, T-VEC may be offered as initial treatment. Type: Evidence based, benefits outweigh harms; Evidence quality: Low; Strength of recommendation: Weak.

document_sections.heading: Literature review and analysis.
document_sections.content: In OPTIM, T-VEC versus granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor for unresectable and/or metastatic melanoma with injectable lesions significantly improved time to treatment failure (HR, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.32 to 0.54), but not OS (HR, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.62 to 1.00); grade 3 and 4 toxicities increased somewhat. Chesney et al found no significant PFS (HR, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.56 to 1.23; P 5 .35) or OS difference (HR, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.44 to 1.46) for T-VEC plus ipilimumab versus ipilimumab. MASTERKEY-265 compared T-VEC with placebo alongside pembrolizumab and found no significant difference for the reported outcome with HR, 0.86 (95% CI, 0.71 to 1.04), or for OS (HR, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.77 to 1.21). Because MASTERKEY-265 compared T-VEC in the context of a recommended treatment, the document states that recommendation 3.5's evidence quality was reduced from moderate to weak.

document_sections.heading: Clinical interpretation.
document_sections.content: The Panel did not consider T-VEC equivalent to the options in recommendations 3.1 and 3.2: those options had stronger supporting evidence, and T-VEC required treatment-delivery infrastructure. For patients with injectable lesions whose recommended regimens are contraindicated, otherwise unavailable to them, or declined, T-VEC remains a reasonable alternative. MASTERKEY-265's lack of a reported PFS or OS benefit reinforces that position.

document_sections.heading: Other considerations.
document_sections.content: Where possible, clinicians should consider clinical trials before using older, nonrecommended therapies such as IL-2 in later lines. Randomized evidence does not guide treatment after progression on every option in recommendations 3.1, 3.2.1, 3.3, and 3.4.

document_sections.heading: NTRK fusions and tumor agnostic indications.
document_sections.content: US FDA approvals for entrectinib and larotrectinib cover unresectable and/or metastatic solid tumors with NTRK fusions after progression on standard treatment or when no viable alternative exists. This indication can include melanoma progressing after therapies in recommendations 3.1 through 3.4. Testing for NTRK fusion and offering an approved agent if positive may therefore be reasonable. Decisions should account for the estimated 0.2% NTRK-fusion prevalence in cutaneous melanoma reported by an ASCO provisional clinical opinion and the very small number of melanoma patients in the nonrandomized approval studies. Greater NTRK-fusion prevalence has been reported in spitzoid melanoma. The ASCO provisional clinical opinion provides additional guidance on somatic testing.

document_sections.heading: Brain metastases.
document_sections.content: A joint ASCO, SNO, and ASTRO guideline addresses melanoma brain metastases. Its recommendation 2.6 permits ipilimumab plus nivolumab regardless of BRAF status, or dabrafenib plus trametinib for BRAF V600E disease, in asymptomatic brain metastases. If either treatment is used, local therapy may be postponed until intracranial progression (Type: Informal consensus; Evidence quality: Low; Strength of recommendation: Weak). Clinicians should follow that guideline and the ASTRO radiation-therapy guideline endorsed by ASCO. Brain metastases were not formally part of this update's systematic review; the Panel identified no substantial new evidence published after the joint guideline's review.

document_sections.heading: Immune-related toxicities and autoimmune disease.
document_sections.content: Clinicians administering immunotherapy should remain highly alert to immune-related toxicity and use ASCO's comprehensive guidance for identifying and managing it in patients with melanoma.

document_sections.heading: Performance status.
document_sections.content: Performance status matters but is less decisive for choosing melanoma systemic therapy than for regimens such as chemotherapy. When tumor burden chiefly causes poor performance status, immunotherapy or targeted treatment might improve it. When comorbidities are the principal cause, treatment risks require careful consideration.

document_sections.heading: Testing.
document_sections.content: BRAF mutation testing is important for selecting melanoma treatment because recommendations differ by BRAF status. The Panel could not formally recommend other specific tests at this time. In progressing BRAF wild-type disease, repeat BRAF testing may be considered because an earlier false negative is technically possible, although it may rarely help and the Panel knows of no supporting high-quality evidence. NRAS and KIT have been described as driver mutations, particularly in melanoma arising on sun-damaged skin, but evidence on treatments targeting those pathways was insufficient for a formal testing recommendation. The ASCO provisional clinical opinion discusses somatic testing more broadly.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Question 4
document_sections.content: The question concerns systemic treatments, individually or in combination, with demonstrated clinical benefit for adults with noncutaneous melanoma of stage II or greater, including whether clinical characteristics, biomarker status, or melanoma type alter benefit.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 4.1.1
document_sections.content: Patients with HLA-A*02:01-positive metastatic uveal melanoma should be offered tebentafusp at 20 mg once on day 1, 30 mg once on day 8, and 68 mg once weekly thereafter until progression. Type: Evidence based, benefits outweigh harms; Evidence quality: Moderate; Strength of recommendation: Strong.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 4.1.2
document_sections.content: For uveal melanoma outside the population in recommendation 4.1.1, the Panel cannot recommend for or against a particular systemic treatment at present. Clinical-trial participation or referral should be offered where feasible. Type: No recommendation; Evidence quality: Very Low; Strength of recommendation: Not applicable.

document_sections.heading: Literature review and analysis.
document_sections.content: Three uveal-melanoma trials were identified across the earlier guideline and this update. Carvajal 2014 found significantly better PFS with selumetinib than with investigator-selected temozolomide or dacarbazine in metastatic disease (HR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.30 to 0.71), but no OS difference (HR, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.41 to 1.06), and more grade 3 toxicity with selumetinib. The subsequent phase III SUMIT comparison of selumetinib plus dacarbazine against placebo plus dacarbazine found no significant PFS (HR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.48 to 1.27; P 5 .32) or OS difference (HR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.39 to 1.46; P 5 .40). EORTC 18021 compared hepatic intra-arterial (HIA) with intravenous fotemustine for uveal melanoma with liver metastases. An unplanned futility analysis stopped it early at 171 patients. HIA significantly improved PFS (HR, 0.62; 95% CI, 0.45 to 0.84), without an OS difference (HR, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.79 to 1.50). Nathan 2021 compared tebentafusp with investigator-selected pembrolizumab, ipilimumab, or dacarbazine in previously untreated HLA-A*02:01-positive metastatic uveal melanoma. Both OS (HR 0.51; 95% CI, 0.37 to 0.71) and PFS (HR 0.73; 95% CI, 0.58 to 0.94) improved significantly. That study prompted the earlier rapid recommendation update, which this full update supersedes.

document_sections.heading: Clinical interpretation.
document_sections.content: The 2020 guideline could not favor or oppose a specific uveal-melanoma therapy. Nathan 2021 led to a rapid update recommending tebentafusp for HLA-A*02:01-positive metastatic disease. Tebentafusp significantly improved 1-year OS and 6-month PFS. Although grade 3 and 4 adverse events are substantial, they become more manageable over time and do not outweigh observed benefit. Better disease control than in the control arm may account for improved landmark PFS and OS despite a low objective response rate; further research must clarify how benefit relates to conventional solid-tumor response criteria. The 2022 rapid recommendation limited use to previously untreated patients, matching the trial's eligibility. The Panel removed that restriction in this full update because it might needlessly impede access.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 4.2
document_sections.content: Pending further evidence, Panel consensus allows patients with unresectable and/or metastatic mucosal melanoma to receive treatments described in recommendations 3.1 through 3.5. Clinical-trial enrollment or referral should be offered where feasible. Type: Informal consensus; Evidence quality: Very Low; Strength of recommendation: Weak.

document_sections.heading: Literature review and analysis.
document_sections.content: The phase II trial by Lian et al studied resected mucosal melanoma in three adjuvant arms: observation after surgery, high-dose IFN, and temozolomide plus cisplatin. It reported significantly longer relapse-free survival with chemotherapy than IFN (20.8 months v 9.4 months, P < .001) and longer OS (48.7 months v 40.4 months, P < .01), and described improvements relative to observation as well. Grade 3 and 4 toxicity was similar between the active-treatment arms. Two trials primarily enrolling cutaneous melanoma each had 16 or fewer patients with mucosal melanoma and were not analyzed further. CheckMate 238 included 27 such patients; its subgroup analysis could not establish an RFS difference between ipilimumab and nivolumab (HR, 1.57; 95% CI, 0.57 to 4.33). This update found no new qualifying mucosal-melanoma trials. A study by Yan et al comparing bevacizumab with no bevacizumab alongside carboplatin and paclitaxel failed eligibility criteria because its control arm had fewer than 50 patients.

document_sections.heading: Clinical interpretation.
document_sections.content: Despite the RFS and OS improvements in Lian et al, the Panel considered its unusually high absolute median outcomes, small size, and design possible explanations for the findings. Indirect cutaneous-melanoma evidence also made temozolomide plus cisplatin difficult to recommend over potentially superior alternatives. The Panel considered adequately powered anti–PD-1 trials in mucosal melanoma unlikely and therefore retained an expert-opinion recommendation without change. No single staging classification is universally accepted for mucosal melanoma, but the Panel believes recommendations 3.1 through 3.5 remain applicable despite uncertainty in stage equivalence. Nonrandomized findings suggest KIT-positive mucosal disease may respond to imatinib; nevertheless, Panel consensus judged the treatments in recommendations 3.1 through 3.5 more likely to benefit patients with unresectable and/or metastatic mucosal melanoma regardless of KIT status.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 4.3
document_sections.content: For other forms of noncutaneous melanoma, the Panel cannot recommend for or against any particular systemic treatment at present. Patients should be offered clinical-trial participation or referral where possible. Type: No recommendation; Evidence quality: Not applicable; Strength of recommendation: Not applicable.

document_sections.heading: Literature review and analysis.
document_sections.content: Neither the 2020 guideline nor the 2022 update identified randomized trials addressing other forms of noncutaneous melanoma.

document_sections.heading: Clinical interpretation.
document_sections.content: The rarity of these other noncutaneous forms makes high-quality randomized treatment evidence unlikely. Unlike for uveal or mucosal disease, the Panel could not recommend extrapolating cutaneous-melanoma therapies. In unresectable and/or metastatic noncutaneous melanoma lacking another supported treatment or progressing after other therapies, NTRK-fusion testing and, if positive, larotrectinib or entrectinib may be reasonable. NTRK-fusion prevalence in noncutaneous melanoma is not well established.

document_sections.heading: DISCUSSION
document_sections.content: The discussion addresses research in progress, uncertainties about potential equivalence among anti–PD-1 and BRAF/MEK treatments, and the effects of changes to melanoma staging criteria.

document_sections.heading: Ongoing Research
document_sections.content: Several trials expected to finish by 2025 could clarify recommendations. The fully accrued, two-arm phase II EBIN trial (EORTC 1612; NCT03235245) compares 3-month encorafenib plus binimetinib induction followed by ipilimumab 1 mg/kg once every three weeks plus nivolumab 3 mg/kg once every three weeks against that ipilimumab–nivolumab regimen alone in BRAF-mutated unresectable stage III or IV melanoma; PFS results were expected in 2023. STOP-GAP (NCT02821013) compares intermittent and continuous anti–PD-1 treatment in metastatic melanoma and was due to finish in 2023. COWBOY (NCT02968303) compares induction vemurafenib plus cobimetinib followed by nivolumab plus ipilimumab with nivolumab plus ipilimumab alone for unresectable and/or metastatic BRAF V600E/K–mutated melanoma; completion was due in 2022. STARBOARD/KEYNOTE-B80 (NCT04657991) compares encorafenib plus binimetinib with placebo alongside pembrolizumab for unresectable and/or metastatic BRAF V600E/K–mutated stage IIIB-D/IV melanoma and was due to finish in 2024. NCT03978611 compares continuing vemurafenib plus cobimetinib beyond progression with second-line nivolumab or pembrolizumab in unresectable and/or metastatic BRAF V600–mutated disease; completion was due in 2023. NADINA (NCT04949113) compares neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab with adjuvant nivolumab in resectable stage III disease and was due to finish in 2025. RELATIVITY-098 (NCT05002569) compares relatlimab plus nivolumab with nivolumab after resection of stage III-IV melanoma and was due to finish in 2025.

document_sections.heading: Anti–PD-1 Therapy Potential Equivalence
document_sections.content: Whether nivolumab and pembrolizumab can be treated as equivalent remained unresolved. They have similar mechanisms, with broadly similar efficacy and toxicity across multiple cancers and trials, but no randomized direct comparison exists and one is unlikely. In some settings the Panel accepted extrapolation, including pembrolizumab as an option for resected stage IV melanoma in recommendation 2.5; it did not extend that reasoning to pembrolizumab plus ipilimumab or pembrolizumab plus relatlimab. The Panel took a conservative approach while acknowledging that others may judge the evidence for equivalence differently.

document_sections.heading: BRAF/MEK Inhibitor Potential Equivalence
document_sections.content: The three BRAF/MEK combinations have similar mechanisms but differing pharmacokinetics, and a future direct trial comparison is highly unlikely. Differences in benefit or toxicity are possible, yet randomized evidence neither supports nor refutes them, and network meta-analyses are inconclusive. The Panel therefore kept its recommendations close to the trial evidence.

document_sections.heading: Changes in Staging Criteria
document_sections.content: Many relevant trials preceded the change from seventh to eighth edition AJCC criteria. Under the eighth edition, mitotic rate no longer determines T1 stage, although it remains prognostically important and should be recorded for T1T4 primary cutaneous melanoma. Regional nodal involvement is classified as clinically occult when found microscopically in a sentinel node, or clinically detected by examination or imaging. Stage III substages combine primary-tumor and nodal features, but reported trials did not stratify by this newer subdivision; benefit by current substage therefore cannot be assessed accurately. Microsatellite and in-transit cutaneous or subcutaneous metastases are stratified by the number of involved lymph nodes. Distant disease is subdivided by site, with serum lactate dehydrogenase further defining categories and a fourth category reflecting central nervous system metastasis. The Panel used eighth edition AJCC stages where possible, particularly in recommendations, although numerous trial descriptions use the seventh edition. It judged the discrepancy important but not destructive to the recommendations' value.

document_sections.heading: PATIENT AND CLINICIAN COMMUNICATION
document_sections.content: Clinical expertise is important when explaining diagnosis and treatment and inviting patients into trials. Information that gives patients agency may support motivation, active participation, adherence, and coping. Communication should address adverse-effect management: effects differ by patient and treatment, and persistent grade 1 events such as fatigue can markedly affect quality of life. Plans for lasting effects should be discussed, especially when care passes to family or primary-care clinicians. ASCO and ESMO provide guidance on immune-related effects, and ASCO provides fatigue guidance. Trial information and enrollment opportunities may differ between community and academic settings; clinicians should learn about relevant trials and may direct patients to local, regional, or national support groups. ASCO's Cancer.Net describes organizations in the United States, and its patient–clinician communication consensus guideline provides additional strategies.

document_sections.heading: HEALTH DISPARITIES
document_sections.content: Access to high-quality cancer care is limited for many patients. In the United States, racial and ethnic minorities with cancer disproportionately encounter comorbidities, barriers to care, lack of insurance, and poorer-quality care; geography and distance also restrict access. Clinicians should account for these inequities and strive to deliver high-quality care to vulnerable groups. Evidence indicates lower cutaneous-melanoma incidence in dark- than light-pigmented skin. African Americans are often diagnosed at noncutaneous sites, including mucosal and acral sites; studies of these subtypes offer an opportunity to address that pattern. Melanoma is also often identified later, potentially increasing morbidity and mortality.

document_sections.heading: MULTIPLE CHRONIC CONDITIONS
document_sections.content: Developing specific evidence-based care recommendations for people with two or more chronic conditions is difficult because their clinical circumstances vary widely. Trials may exclude them to avoid interactions and confounding, limiting how reliably trial outcomes apply. For patients with multiple conditions, treatment and follow-up planning should account for that complexity and uncertainty through shared decisions. Clinicians should review and consider every other chronic condition when applying recommendations for melanoma.

document_sections.heading: COST IMPLICATIONS
document_sections.content: The 2020 guideline included a nonsystematic review of cost-effectiveness literature and discussed treatment costs there.

document_sections.heading: EXTERNAL REVIEW AND OPEN COMMENT
document_sections.content: Draft recommendations were open for public comment from February 27 through March 13, 2023. For individual recommendations, the lowest full-agreement proportion was 63%, many exceeded >75%, and the highest disagreement proportion was 10%. The Panel considered the responses and clarified several clinical interpretations before review and approval. Two external content reviewers also commented on details and expressed confidence in the guideline's quality; their feedback was incorporated before final approval.

document_sections.heading: GUIDELINE IMPLEMENTATION
document_sections.content: ASCO develops its guidelines for use across care settings and includes a Practice Guideline Implementation Network (PGIN) representative to assess community applicability and identify barriers. Such barriers include limited awareness among frontline clinicians, survivors, and caregivers, and insufficient services where resources are constrained. The Bottom Line summary was designed to assist implementation, with distribution through PGIN and publication through ASCO channels. ASCO considers clinical trials important for informing decisions and improving cancer care and supports an opportunity for every patient to participate.

document_sections.heading: ADDITIONAL RESOURCES
document_sections.content: The guideline identifies supplementary evidence tables, slide sets, clinical tools, and patient information as resources accompanying its recommendations.

document_sections.heading: GENDER-INCLUSIVE LANGUAGE
document_sections.content: ASCO seeks care that supports people regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. Transgender and nonbinary people may face stigmatization, invisibility, and exclusion in oncology care; language that assumes a link between sex and anatomy can contribute to inaccessibility. The authors therefore use gender-inclusive terms where possible while reporting the characteristics of gender-specific research as those studies reported them.

document_sections.heading: APPENDIX
document_sections.content: TABLE A1 defines recommendation strength and evidence quality. A Strong recommendation favors an intervention when desirable effects outweigh undesirable ones, or opposes it when undesirable effects outweigh desirable ones; all or almost all informed people would make the recommended choice. A Weak recommendation reflects probable net benefit or harm with appreciable uncertainty; most informed people would choose the stated course, but a substantial number would not. High evidence quality denotes strong confidence that the true effect is near the estimate. Moderate denotes moderate confidence, while allowing a substantially different true effect. Low denotes limited confidence and the possibility of a substantially different effect. Very low denotes very little confidence, with the true effect likely to differ substantially from the estimate.
